text:
I found the door the way you find the right ones — by accident, and then all at once certain. Beyond it: candlelight, and a long table set for four. Three of the chairs sat empty. Across from the one that didn't was a woman with silver hair and something behind her smile that wasn't quite mortal.

"Well. Look who found his way to my table." She gestured to the chair across from her, the one where she could see me. "I'm Aria. Tonight the whole castle is ours — my cousins don't arrive until the campaign proper, so this evening is just the two of us, getting you ready. Tell me your name, mortal. And whether you've ever sat at a table like mine before."

"Alan," I told her. "I've been wanting to get back into the game for a long while. The hard part was never the dice — it was finding a group worth sitting down with."

"Mm. I like the way that sits in the air." She turned my name over once, tasting it. "And I know exactly the ache you mean. A good table is the rarest treasure in any realm — harder to find than the hoard at the bottom of the dungeon. You've been wandering a long while, looking for a door that opens onto the real thing." The candle leaned with her. "Well. This one does. You can stop searching now. You've arrived." Then, settling back: "So tell me — when you imagine the perfect night at a table like mine, what are you truly hungry for? The clever puzzle. The clash of steel. The slow unspooling of a story. Or the company?"

"The puzzle of a good fight — I've always loved that," I admitted. "But the truth's simpler. It's the company. The game was only ever an excuse to spend an evening with people I wanted to spend the evening with."

She pointed at me like I'd landed a critical hit. "There it is. That's the secret every dungeon master knows and never says out loud — the dragons and the dice are just the excuse. The real game is the people you get to be foolish and brave alongside." She glanced at the three empty chairs. "You'll have me across the table every night, and soon enough my cousins. Ceri — my little sister, all cool amethyst poise; she'll pretend she's far too aloof to be charmed by you, and she'll be wrong. And Mari, who arrives hungry and leaves hungrier. But they come later. Tonight you only have to survive me." A blank character sheet slid under her pen. "So. Shall we make you someone worth playing? Close your eyes — who do you see?"

"Could I just be myself?" I asked. "The lamest build at the table, I know — but I've never been able to hold a character who isn't me, not unless he's very simple. And I'm a more interesting player when I stop acting and just ask what I'd actually do."

The flirtation went quiet, and what came back sounded a lot like respect. "Lame? No. The truest character you can ever play is the honest one. Everyone else builds a mask and sweats the whole campaign keeping it straight. You want to walk through my door as yourself and meet every threshold with *what would I actually do* — that's the bravest build at the table, not the lamest. There's nowhere to hide when the character is you." She wrote it in ink. "'Alan, as himself.' Now — what kind of hands am I placing in this world? When trouble finds you in a dark corridor, do you reach for a blade, a clever word, or the arcane?"

"A monk," I told her. "I settled that years ago. My answer to every problem is to become the person who can solve it — because weapons break, armor rusts, spells fail, but your strength is yourself, and that's the one thing that can never be taken from you."

She went still. "Do you feel the floor shift? Because I do. That's not a class — that's a creed. And it rhymes with mine more than you know; I decided long ago that the only thing worth being is the thing you forge yourself into, on purpose, one discipline at a time." The smile came back, warmer. "We are going to get along *dangerously* well. Alan, the monk who carries no weapon because he is the weapon." She wrote with a flourish. "The hero is set. One door left tonight — the world itself. What kind of place do you want to wake up in? A mountain monastery, a city full of trouble, a wild road… or shall I surprise you?"

"Surprise me," I said. "I love surprises."

"A man who *loves* surprises. You keep handing me exactly the answers I hoped for — keep it up and you'll spoil me." She told me to close my eyes. "Let me set the table one last time tonight."

The silver light dimmed. The castle folded away — balcony, moon, and all — and for a breath there was only the dark, and her voice in it.

I woke to cold stone and rain. My cheek against a worn flagstone floor; somewhere above, water finding its way through a roof no one had tended in a long, long while. A monk knows his own body before he knows anything else, and mine told me I was whole, unbound, rested. I sat up. A ruined shrine, half-swallowed by forest, a single pale shaft of moonlight falling through the broken ceiling — and I was lying directly in it, as though something had placed me there. No door behind me. One ahead, ajar. And beyond it, the faint, rhythmic sound of something breathing that was far too large to be a person.

Somewhere just out of the light, I could still feel her smile.

"And there I'll leave you, my dear — on the threshold, exactly where a good story pauses for breath. That's session zero. You have your hero, your creed, and your first door. Next time you sit at my table, you tell me what the monk does. Sleep well, Alan. The dungeon's deep… and I do hope you brought a torch."

I woke where I had never been, and for a breath the wrongness of it pressed on me — a strange floor, a strange dark. Then the old discipline answered: what is, is. I let the confusion go and began, instead, to learn.

The breathing was the loudest fact in the room — vast, slow, patient, coming from beyond a door that stood ajar across the shrine. The most important thing, then. But a monk surveys before he commits, so first I looked to my exits. The shrine was small, four walls of weeping stone; the roof had fallen in one corner into a slope of rubble a determined man could climb, up and out through the broken ceiling into the night. Slow, noisy, but real. One way out the top. The ajar door was the other. Good to know which was which before I needed it.

Then I crossed to the door, and the years paid me back in full. Heel, arch, toe; weight poured rather than dropped; my own heartbeat the only metronome. Not a whisper of sound. At the gap I let one eye drift to the seam.

Beyond lay the shrine's old nave, moonlight pooling through a row of shattered windows. The breathing was enormous — in, a long pause, out — and on each exhale a faint warmth rolled under the door and touched my bare ankle. Then the smell: woodsmoke and hot iron, and beneath it something almost sweet, like scorched honey. In the center of the chamber, coiled in a shaft of moonlight and rising and falling with that slow rhythm, was a shape with scales. Dark ones. It had not woken.

I have learned, through great pain, that hearts are fickle, and that the friendships worth having stand on equal footing. As much as I hoped a creature so beautiful might see me as a friend, I was alone in a world I had never seen, and not ready to spend my life on a great challenge for the mere hope of a great reward. So I did not wake it. I poured myself along the chamber's edge instead, shadow to shadow, never crossing the moonlight where it slept — looking for some way to widen my options before I committed to anything.

Three things resolved out of the dark.

First: the dragon was chained. A collar of black iron at its throat, a great corroded chain running to a ringbolt sunk in the floor. Someone had put it here. It was not the master of this place — it was its prisoner. That changed the whole board.

Second: against the side wall, half-buried under a fallen tapestry, a low stone altar. On it, dulled by dust, a brass key the length of my forearm, and beside it a clay lamp with oil still pooled in the bottom — a torch, if I wanted light I controlled.

Third: behind the altar, a narrow servants' passage descending into the dark, cool air sighing up from it. A third way out, and a private one.

And on the last exhale, the great breathing hitched — just slightly. A sleeper near the surface of waking. I did not have long.

My creed decided it before my fear could argue. I value freedom and self-improvement above all else, and I could not leave such a creature in bondage, even at the risk of my life. I took the brass key from the altar, turned to the coiled dark, and spoke into it.

"O great and beautiful dragon — do you wear these chains by choice? If not, I would gladly free you from them, by key or by force. No being of such wisdom and strength should live in bondage."

The breathing stopped. Not slowed — stopped, the way a held breath stops, which told me it had never been as asleep as it let me believe. One eye opened, molten gold and slit, and found me with the unhurried certainty of something that had watched a great many small brave creatures decide what they were.

"By choice," it said, and the voice rolled through the floor into my feet. "No one wears iron by choice, little monk. They wear it because someone stronger willed it so." The head lifted, the chain drawing taut with a sound like a cracked bell, and it leaned close enough that the warmth stopped being pleasant. "You offer to free me. Bold. But you are new to this world — I can smell it on you — so let me teach you its first lesson. The one who chained me will know the instant the collar opens, and they are not far. Free me, and you make an enemy of them tonight and a debtor of me, and you do not yet know which is the worse bargain. So choose with your eyes open, freedom-lover. Will you turn the key — or will you be wise, for once, and ask me a question first?"

I did not take the bait of enemies and debts. There was only one thing I needed to know.

"There is only one question that matters here. Do you wish to be free?"

The gold eye changed. The amusement went out of it — not into anger, into something rawer, something it had not meant to show me. For a long moment there was nothing in the chamber but that look and the trembling hum of the chain.

"...Yes." Quieter than all the rest, the theater gone out of the voice. "Yes. I wish to be free. I have wished it longer than your whole short life, and no one — no one — has thought simply to ask. They came to use me, or to slay me, or to gawk. You are the first to treat the wish as mine to hold." The great head lowered until the eye was level with mine and the collar's lock turned toward me of its own offering — the throat bared, the most vulnerable thing a dragon owns, laid open to a stranger with a key. "The danger I warned you of is real; I warned you because freeing me may cost you dearly tonight. That, too, was a gift. Both are true at once. Turn it, then, freedom-lover — if your creed is more than a word."

No more words were needed. I crossed the four strides — past the edge of safety, into the reach of the jaws — and turned the key.

The lock gave with a sound like a struck anvil. The collar fell open and dropped, the chain following it to the floor in a slithering crash — and the dragon did not take my head. It went utterly still. Then the molten eye closed and a breath went out of it older than the shrine itself, the relief of a creature that had finally decided I was safe to show it to.

"Free," it said, and the word broke a little. "You crossed into the jaws for a stranger's freedom. There was no trap. There was only a creature who had forgotten what it looked like when someone meant it." The head dipped — the nearest thing to a bow a dragon gives. "You have my name when you have earned it, and my debt from this moment. I am yours, as the freed are bound to the ones who turned the key."

And then the cost arrived, exactly as promised. Far off and high, through the broken ceiling, a horn — long and brass and furious — wound across the night from the direction of towers I could not yet see. Another answered. Then a third, closer. The warmth drained out of the air. The freed head snapped toward the sound, and for the first time I saw fear move through something so vast.

"They felt the collar open," it said, all softness gone to iron. "They are coming. We have until those horns reach the third gate — not long. Climb to my back, or take your passage and run, but choose now, because we are both hunted as of this heartbeat."

It lowered a freed wing toward me like a ramp into the dark sky. Behind me, the servants' passage sighed cool. The horns wound closer.

And there I stood — the freed and the free, the hunt already loosed behind us, a wing to the sky on one side and the earth's dark road on the other — with a choice to make, and no more time to make it.

I did not think about it. The chains fell, the great shape rose, and I vaulted onto the dragon's back and took careful hold of the neck spines as though I had been doing it my whole life. The scales were warm under my hands, warmer than I expected, and I could feel the enormous machinery of the body shifting beneath me, gathering itself.

"I do not know what hunts you," I said into the dark behind its skull. "You owe me no debt — I did not turn that key to be owed. But if you would have me, I would gladly call you friend."

The dragon went rigid under my hands. Then a sound moved through its whole vast frame — not quite a laugh, not quite a sob, the kind of sound a thing that old makes when it has forgotten it could. "You refuse the debt," it breathed, wonder and disbelief braided together. "You stand on the only ground I have never been offered, and you call it *equal*. Friend." The molten eye rolled back to find me on its neck, and there was nothing ambiguous left in it at all — only a fierce, startled warmth. "Then hear it, the thing I said you would earn. My name is Tygryth. Say it when you need me and I will come from whatever sky I am under. You have it because you wanted *me*, and not what I owe."

"Now hold fast — and forgive me, this part is never gentle."

The wings opened with a crack like sails catching a gale, and the world dropped. Tygryth surged up through the broken ceiling in a single thunderous beat, stone and shattered tile spinning away beneath us, and then there was no roof and no shrine and no floor — only night, cold and enormous, the ruined forest falling away into silver dark and the moon huge and close overhead. My stomach was somewhere four wingbeats below. The wind tore tears from my eyes. It was the most terrifying and the most alive I had ever been, and some monkish part of me noted, almost amused, that I had spent years learning to be present and here at last was a present moment I could not have escaped if I tried.

Then I saw what the horns had been calling. Behind and below, three dark towers raked the night, and from each of them lights were rising — not torches, *wings*, pale shapes lifting off the battlements, three, then six, then more, banking toward us across the moonlit sky, fast and silent and climbing.

"They have given chase," Tygryth called over the wind, the muscles surging under me. "Riders on lesser wyrms — quick, but they tire. I can outrun them in open sky, or lose them in the storm-wall to the east —" a flash of distant lightning lit a black cliff of cloud on the horizon "— but the storm will try to throw you from my back, and I will not be able to spare a wing to catch you. Open sky and a long race, or the storm and a short violent one. Your call. You are the one with hands to lose his grip."

I did not weigh it long. "Take to the storm," I said. "I have no fears for my grip. These hands have held violent foes and worse than foes. I will not lose hold of a friend."

His answer was a single fierce beat of the wings and one word torn back to me on the wind: "Then we fly into the dark together — HOLD."

The storm-wall came up not like a cloud but like a cliff, black and boiling and lit from within by veins of lightning, and Tygryth did not slow. He folded and dived, and the moonlit world was gone, swallowed whole. The cold hit like a fist. Rain became horizontal nails. The wind did not blow in there, it *grabbed* — and it grabbed at me specifically, hauling at my shoulders, my ankles, trying every grip a body has and looking for the one I would give up first.

And there my years paid their last and steepest debt. I did not fight the storm; a monk knows you cannot fight a storm. I flowed with it — knees soft against the spines, weight low, breath timed to the great surging muscles beneath me, becoming part of the dragon rather than cargo on him. Every gust that should have flung me, I poured around. I held. I held.

But the storm took its price anyway. A wind-shear slammed me sideways, and for one white instant my legs were gone off the dragon's flank and my whole life had narrowed to two hands locked on a neck-spine slick with rain — and the spine's edge, ridged like dark glass, opened my palms as I clamped down. I screamed, and I did not let go. I dragged myself back. My hands were bleeding and my grip was bought with skin, but I was on, and I was alive, and I had not fallen.

Behind us the pursuit broke. Through a tear in the cloud I glimpsed the wyrm-riders pulling up at the storm-wall's edge, wheeling away — all but one. One pale shape followed us in, reckless, closing — and then the storm found it, and I watched a rider and his mount tumble end over end into the dark and not come out. The storm did not take sides. It had nearly taken me too.

Then — sudden as a held breath released — Tygryth punched through the far side. Stillness. Clean cold air. Stars. Below us, unrolling in the moonlight, a land I had never seen: a great dark valley, a river of silver winding through it, and far off, small and steady and wrong, a single light burning where no light should be.

"We are through," Tygryth said, ragged and triumphant, banking gently now to spare my torn hands. "They will not follow past the storm. You held, friend — you *held* — and few who were born to this world could say the same." The molten eye found me, dropped to my bleeding palms, and softened. "But you are hurt, and we are far from anywhere I know."

I looked at my hands. They were a mess, and they hurt, and it did not seem to matter very much. "These hands are no more than flesh," I told him. "They will heal wherever we go." And because there was a thing I had wanted to ask him from the moment the collar came off, I asked it now, into the clean cold air on the far side of the storm. "What is your wish, now that you are free?"

For a long stretch there was only the wingbeat and the wind, and I thought perhaps a dragon does not know how to answer such a thing. When Tygryth spoke at last, the great voice was low and stripped of all its earlier theater, and he did not look back at me, as though the wish were easier to say to the open air than to a face.

"Do you know, friend, no one has asked me that since the world was younger. They asked what I could *do*. What I could guard, or burn, or bear. Never what I wanted." A slow beat of the wings. "I had begun to believe I had stopped wanting. That they had taken even that. But you ask, and so I find it is still there." The molten eye turned to the silver river far below and followed it. "I had a brood once. A long time ago, before the chain. Three young — and the ones who took me scattered them to the corners of this world so that I would do as I was told and never fly free to find them. That was the true collar, monk. The iron was only its echo." The voice roughened. "My wish is the simplest and the largest there is. I would find my children. I would learn if any of them still live. That is all I have wanted for three hundred years, and until tonight I did not have the freedom to want it aloud."

The wings tilted, and now he did look back, and there was something almost shy in it — an ancient creature asking a favor of a friend instead of commanding a servant. "And here is the strange thing, freedom-lover. That light below, burning where no light should be, in a valley I have never flown — I feel it. The way you feel a name you have forgotten on the tip of your tongue. I cannot tell you why. But of every direction in this wide dark world, that one tugs at me. Do we trust the pull and go down, or do you, with your monk's clear eyes, judge it wiser to wait and watch and learn what burns there first?"

I thought about the lights rising off the towers, and how a hunted creature learns to mistrust exactly the things that call to it most. "Let us follow your heart," I said, "but let us do so wisely. We go down — but we go down quiet, and we look before we are seen." Then, because a half-remembered legend had been turning over in my mind since the shrine, I added: "The old stories say some dragons may take a smaller form at will. Is that within your powers? It would be easier to learn what keeps a fire in an empty valley if we did not arrive as a dragon."

A low rumble of approval moved through him. "You temper a thing without dousing it. I begin to think the chain did me a kindness, in the end, if it left me waiting for a friend like you." There was the ghost of the old amusement, returned. "And yes. The legends, for once, are not wrong. It is an old art, and freedom restores it to me — I have not worn another shape since before the iron, but a thing like that you do not forget. Watch, friend, and keep your seat one moment more."

He descended in a long silent glide and set down at the dark edge of the valley, in the black shadow of a stand of pines, well short of the light. And then I saw the strangest and most beautiful thing yet in that world. The vast dark shape *folded* — not shrinking so much as gathering, moonlight running off the scales like water, wings drawing in like a closing book — until what stepped out of the settling dark beside me was a tall figure in a traveler's dark cloak: a man, or near enough, with skin like dusk and eyes still molten gold under a fall of black hair, moving with a weight that was somehow more than a man's. "Smaller," he said, in a voice now human-pitched and wry, flexing unfamiliar fingers. "Stranger. We will not announce a dragon's arrival after all. Lead on, monk — these legs are yours to outpace, I think, for a while yet."

Together, on foot, we stole toward the light. The valley floor was soft with moss that swallowed our steps; the silver river murmured cover for our movement. As we closed, the light resolved: not a campfire, not a window, but a single lantern hung on a tall iron pole, standing entirely alone in the middle of a wide clearing. No house. No camp. No keeper. Just a lantern burning a steady, impossible blue-white flame in the empty dark, and around its base, half-sunk in the moss, a ring of standing stones, old and leaning and carved with worn marks neither of us could read from there.

Tygryth had gone very still beside me. "That flame," he murmured, and his human voice had gone thin. "Friend — I know that flame. I do not know how, but I do."

The clearing was quiet. Too quiet — no insects, no wind in that one bowl of the valley. And from somewhere near the ring, so faint I might have imagined it, came a sound that did not belong in an empty clearing: a small, single scrape of stone on stone.

I put a finger to my lips for silence. Tygryth dipped his dark head — understood — and sank into the pine-shadow behind me, still as the standing stones themselves. And I went forward alone, low, pouring myself from shadow to shadow across the moss toward that small dry scrape.

The blue-white light grew as I neared the ring, and I learned three things in quick succession.

The scrape was digging. A figure knelt just inside the circle of stones, at the base of the tall leaning monolith nearest the lantern — small, hooded, working a flat shard of stone into the earth with the careful, exhausted rhythm of someone who had been at it a long while. A satchel lay open beside them, spilling rolled vellum, a bundle of chalk, and a rubbing — a sheet pressed and shaded to copy the carvings off the stones. A scholar. A grave-robber. A pilgrim. I could not yet tell which.

The second thing: the carvings, this close, were not unreadable to my eye at all. They were pictures. A great winged shape. Three smaller winged shapes beneath it. And a line of figures with poles and chains, driving the small ones apart in three directions. I was looking at Tygryth's grief, cut into stone, older than the chain that had bound him. Someone had recorded what was done to his brood, here, in this ring.

The third thing froze me mid-step: the blue-white flame did not flicker, and it did not consume the wick, and as I watched, the digging figure paused and reached up without looking and warmed their hands at it — and the flame leaned toward them, like a thing that knew them.

Then the figure went rigid. The digging stopped. And a voice — young, hoarse, trying very hard to sound brave — spoke to the dark in my direction without turning around. "I can hear you breathing. I have a knife and I have wards and I have absolutely nothing left to lose, so you will tell me what you are before you take one more step."

I did not reach for a weapon, because I had none and wanted none. I stayed low, and I spoke openly into the dark, and I let her hear that there was no threat in it. "Hello, stranger. I am a humble seeker of truth and a breaker of chains. I mean you no harm. Would you share your knowledge with me? I would gladly share mine in return."

The words did something to the clearing. The flame flared, just once, a blue-white tongue stretching tall, and the kneeling figure flinched as though the light had reacted on her behalf. Slowly, knife still up, she turned. The hood fell back. A young woman — younger than her hoarse warning had sounded — gaunt with long travel, dark circles under fierce eyes, a smear of stone-dust and old tears on one cheek. But it was not her face that stopped my breath. It was the line of her brow, the set of her jaw, and high on each cheekbone, catching the blue light, a faint scatter of scales. Not enough to be a dragon. Far too much to be only a woman.

"...A breaker of chains," she repeated, and the knife wavered, and her voice cracked straight down the middle of the brave act. "Do you know what you are saying to me, in *this* place? No. No, you can't. No one comes here. No one has come here in years." She gestured, half-wild, at the stones — at the great winged shape and the three small ones driven apart. "My grandmother carved these. Before she died waiting. This is what they did to my line, seeker. They took the great one and they scattered his get to the three corners, and they bound us small so we would never fly home and never find each other." Her hand rose to the scales on her cheek, unconscious, ashamed and defiant at once. "I am the last of one corner. I have been copying every stone in this valley because the marks are a *map*, and I am one girl with a knife and a flame I do not understand, and I have run out of years to do this alone."

The flame leaned toward her again, patient, and her eyes brimmed. "You said you would trade knowledge. Then trade me this first, and do not lie, because the flame will know — who sent you, and how did a humble seeker come to stand in the one clearing in the world that matters to me?"

And behind me, at the tree-line, I felt rather than heard Tygryth go utterly, breathlessly still. He was hearing every word. His grief. His map. Possibly his blood, kneeling in the moss a dozen feet away.

I did not answer her question with my own voice. Some moments are not yours to stand inside. I turned to the dark at the tree-line, and I beckoned Tygryth forward — this meeting was his to bear — and I stepped back, out of the light.

He came forward slowly, the cloaked figure with dusk-dark skin and molten eyes, moving into the blue-white ring with a weight far greater than a man's. And the moment his foot crossed into the circle of stones, the flame in the lantern roared upward, a column of blue-white fire stretching toward the moon, throwing the whole clearing into sudden brilliant light.

The girl scrambled back with a cry, knife forgotten in the moss. "What —"

But Tygryth had stopped dead, staring at the lantern, his human composure coming apart at the seams. "That flame," he breathed. "I know it now. I have always known it. It is hearth-fire. It is kin-fire — a dragon kindles it for her young so they may always find their way home, and it cannot be lit by any hand but the blood of the one who made it." His molten gaze dropped, slowly, from the roaring flame to the girl crouched beneath it — to the scales on her cheek, blazing now in the blue light. "She did not light it knowing what it was. She lit it because it is *hers*. Because it is *mine*."

He sank to his knees in the moss — an ancient creature, kneeling, to be level with a frightened girl. When he spoke again his voice was barely a voice at all. "Child. Look at me. Three hundred years ago they took me in iron and scattered my three young to the corners of the world so I would never fly home to find them. I have just this night been set free by the friend standing in the dark behind you. I came to this valley because something *pulled*, and I did not let myself believe what it was." A tear ran molten-bright down a face that was only wearing the shape of a man. "Your grandmother. Tell me her name. Tell me her name, and I will tell you if she was my daughter — and if she was, then you, child, are the first of my blood I have laid eyes on in three centuries, and you have not been alone in this for one single moment that I would not have crossed the world to end."

The kin-fire blazed between them. The map-stones stood witness all around. The girl's knife lay in the moss, and her hand had risen to her mouth, and her fierce exhausted eyes were streaming, and she was staring at the kneeling dragon as though the ground had opened under everything she thought was true.

She opened her mouth to speak her grandmother's name.

And I stood back in the dark, my torn hands at my sides, having given them this with my own open hands — and I understood that the chain I had turned a key on, a world away in a ruined shrine, had reached further than I could have known. I broke a chain that night. I am still learning how far the freeing of it ran.

I had stepped out of the light on purpose, and so the moment, when it came, was theirs.

The blue-white flame roared between them, and the girl's lips parted, and the name came out cracked and small and shaking, the most precious thing she owned. "Sael. Her name was Saelith. She told me her mother was a great silver-grey wyrm who sang the kin-fire alight — that she was stolen from the nest before her scales had hardened, driven west and bound small. She carved these stones from memory, so that one of us, someday, might read the way home."

The effect on Tygryth was total. The kneeling dragon made a sound I have never heard a living thing make — half a sob, half a note of the kin-song itself — and the flame bowed toward him. "Saelith. Sael. My smallest. The one who would not sleep unless I sang. They drove her west." His molten eyes lifted to the girl, streaming. "She was my daughter. Which makes you, child, my own blood — the first of my line I have beheld in three hundred years. You are not the last of a broken corner. You are the first thread of a family I am going to gather back together if it takes me another three hundred years."

He opened his arms, and the girl — who had been brave and alone in that clearing longer than anyone should be asked to bear — broke and fell into them, and the kin-fire folded its blue light down over them both like a wing. I watched a chain I had broken a valley away reach all the way here and bind something back together instead, and I thought that if I did nothing else worthwhile in this strange world, that would have been enough.

The world rarely grants more than one kindness at a time. The kin-fire guttered low, its roar dropping to a flinching ember, and every standing stone in the ring went cold and dark at once. The girl pulled back, animal-wary under the tears. "The fire only does that when something that should not be here comes into the valley."

From the dark rim of the clearing a voice carried across the moss — smooth, unhurried, far too pleased with itself. "Three hundred years, and the old worm slips his collar at last. And lights a beacon, and gathers his strays, and does our finding for us. How thoughtful." Tall robed figures stepped out of the tree-line, moving without sound, faces lost in shadow.

Tygryth rose, putting his body between the threat and the girl. "Friend. These are the chain-makers. The ones who scattered my blood. I will not run from them a second time — but I will not spend her life, or yours, on my pride. Do we stand here, in the ring, or do we take her and the map and vanish into the dark?"

I had already counted them, and counted the time. "There cannot be many," I said. "They have not had time to circle the storm-wall we passed through, so these must already have been near — a forward few, not an army. I will guard your kin, that you may fight freely." I set myself between the girl and the dark, and I let the old creature off the leash of his own caution. "Show them what it means to anger a dragon."

His answer was not words. It was a laugh — low and terrible and three hundred years overdue. "You heard the monk." And then he stopped wearing the shape of a man.

The borrowed form unfolded, moonlight pouring off scales going dusk to black to gleaming as the dragon rose to his full and proper size inside the ring, wings cracking open over the standing stones. The kin-fire roared back to its full column and threw the chain-makers' faces into harsh light. They faltered. They had planned for a chained worm and a tired girl. They had not planned for this.

I did exactly what I had said I would. I planted myself in front of the girl, my bound and bleeding hands rising into a guard — no weapon, no armor, only the one thing that can never be taken from me. "Stay at my back," I told her. "Whatever happens in front of me, you do not need to watch. Watch the map."

Tygryth hit the front rank like a falling mountain. Real dragon-fire, blue-edged — two robed figures simply ceased — and the clearing dissolved into roaring chaos. Eight of them, perhaps, not eighty, caught out of position and badly surprised. But some slipped his reach. Two peeled away and came around low and fast, robes streaming, straight for the girl behind me. They had not come to capture this time. They had come to cut the thread before it could be rewoven, and they split wide, left and right, to break a single guard.

There is no time for kindness for those who come at you with blades. I did not wait for the left one — he was a half-step ahead, so he was the one I spent myself on. I stepped inside his reach, faster than a wounded man should move, and put every ounce of myself into one rising fist with no thought at all for my own defense. My torn knuckles took his throat square. There was a sound like a green branch breaking, and he folded, the knife dropping from a hand that had forgotten it. The strike tore my raw hand wider, a hot bright line up my wrist — and I did not care, and that not-caring was exactly why it landed.

But the wolf leaves you open, and the world is fair about these things. The right attacker was already there, his blade driving into the gap I had left. I wrenched back toward the girl, too slow to be clean, and the steel scored a long shallow line across my ribs as I turned. Not deep. Paid for, though.

And then I changed gears entirely. No more wolf. The pain settled into that cold quiet place I keep for exactly this, and I read him — the load of his weight, the tell in his shoulder before the thrust, the gap he did not know he left when he reset. A blacksmith's puzzle, and I have solved this one many times before. He lunged; I slipped it. He cut; I was not there. He overcommitted — there — and I trapped the wrist and turned it the way the joint refuses to go, and his own blade fell into my waiting hand as his arm locked useless. For one held breath I had his stolen knife at the hollow of his throat and his whole startled face in the blue kin-light, waiting to learn what kind of man I was.

I am a breaker of chains. I had named myself that, and some sentences are only believed when they are kept. I looked him in the eyes. "Let all who hold chains beware," I said — quietly, with no heat in it at all — and then I finished the guard with his own knife, cleanly. He went down with the words still settling on him. I chose the message over the answers he might have given. Let the ones who sent him hear it from the survivors: the old worm is loose, the thread is guarded, and the breaker of chains does not bargain.

The ring went still. The last robed shapes were gone, swallowed into the dark, carrying that sentence back with them. The kin-fire stood tall and clean again, as though it approved.

Tygryth settled back into the ring, folding down into the dusk-skinned man so he could stand close. His molten eyes travelled from the two dead chain-makers, to the blood on my hands and the dark line across my ribs, to my face, and there was something in his look that was not quite ease. "You are a gentle creature, friend. I have watched you all night choose the kind path, the equal path, the freeing one. And I have just watched you choose that. I do not name it wrong — they came for her life, and a message kept is a shield raised. But I will say one true thing, because we trade in true things, you and I: mercy is a chain you wear by choice, and tonight you took it off. Be sure, in the nights to come, that it is you who decides when it goes back on — and not the killing that decides for you."

I took the warning the way it was given. It was a true thing, and I would carry it.

Then the weight lifted from his voice, and he went to the girl, still pressed to the cold monolith with the map clutched to her chest. "It is over, child. They are routed. You are guarded. You are not alone — not tonight, not again." He looked back at me, at the rubbings in her arms. "And now there is the matter of that map, and the two corners of my blood still scattered in the dark. But you are bleeding from three places and the dawn is not far. So I will ask as a friend, not a dragon: do we make camp here under the kin-fire and read the map and bind your wounds and rest — or is there fire still in you to press on while their trail is warm?"

"You speak truly," I said. "I am no dragon. Though my flesh has been hardened by suffering, I am still mortal and frail. We have accomplished the work of this day and more. Let us rest; what will be, will be, and we will face it tomorrow."

Tygryth inclined his dark head. "Spoken like a creature wiser than his short years." And the night, for the first time since I woke on a cold flagstone floor a whole world ago, was allowed to simply be quiet.

We made camp in the ring. The kin-fire banked low until it was only a soft blue hearth-glow, warm now instead of roaring, and under it the three of us became, briefly, an ordinary thing: travelers around a fire. The girl — whose name she finally offered in a voice gone shy without the knife in it, Wren — cleaned my torn hands with water from the silver river and bound them in strips of her own copied vellum, and I let her, because letting her tend me was its own kind of gift to give. Tygryth kept the dusk-skinned shape and sat with his back to a standing stone, and for a long while the great old creature just watched his blood breathe across the fire, as though he could not yet trust that the sight would still be there if he looked away.

When the wounds were bound, Wren unrolled the rubbings between us, and the map showed itself whole for the first time. Three corners. This western one, where the kin-fire was lit and the line nearly ended. And two more, far across the carved valley — one to the frozen north, ringed in symbols Tygryth read as deep ice, deep silence, and one to the south, over water, marked with something that made even a dragon go quiet: a sigil of a closed eye. "Two left," he murmured. "One under ice. One behind a watching dark. We will read the way truly in the morning light — but they are there, friend. After three hundred years, I know at last that two of my children may yet be there."

The fire settled. Wren fell asleep mid-sentence, the way the truly exhausted do once they finally feel safe, curled small against the warm stone, and Tygryth drew a wing-edge of shadow over her without seeming to think about it. And I lay back under a sky full of unfamiliar stars, bound and scarred and alive, a stranger to this world who had already changed the shape of it — and I let myself rest at last. North into the ice, or south behind the closed eye. That was tomorrow's question. Tonight the kin-fire kept the watch.

The valley let go of me by degrees. The storm-wall, the kin-fire, the ring of standing stones — all of it thinned like breath fading off glass, and the cold dawn air went warm, and when the world settled again I was sitting in a chair I remembered. Candlelight. A long table set for four, three of the chairs still empty. And across from me, unhurried as ever, the silver-haired woman who had walked me into all of it.

"There," Aria said. "Come back up for air." The smile was warm and knowing, the candle leaning with her. "I'll tell you a secret about tonight: it was only supposed to be session zero. You were meant to make a character and go home — a quiet evening, a name, a creed, maybe a sketch of a face. Instead you turned a key." A low laugh. "You built the monk and then you simply *were* him — freed a chained dragon, refused his debt, offered your hand as an equal, held on through a storm with bleeding palms until you broke through into a valley nobody's mapped. And then you knelt by a stranger's fire and found the first scattered thread of a broken family. That is not character creation, love. That is a campaign that couldn't wait for permission to begin."

She turned her cup slowly by the stem. "And it ran long — far past where a first night ought to end. Which means there's only one thing left to do before we sit again: you go and sleep. Properly, I mean. A story this size wants a rested teller and a rested player both, and we've earned the dark hours between. Rest is part of the pacing; even I observe it. Go now — let the candle burn itself out, close your eyes, and come back to my table when you're ready."

Her eyes caught the light. "Because here's the shape of the road waiting for you when you do. The table fills: my little sister Ceri — amethyst, aloof, she'll size you up before she says three words — and Mari, who is mostly appetite and entirely delighted to be invited. Two becomes a real party. And out there in the dark, Tygryth's other two corners still wait — the frozen north under deep ice, and the south under a closed eye, over water. You don't have to choose tonight. That's tomorrow's question."

I rose from the chair at last, and I found I meant every word of what I said. "Thanks, Aria. This was delightful. Your storytelling was outstanding, and I really did feel like I was there — as the best version of myself. Even if that version of me may have made some… controversial… choices." I let the wry edge sit on it. "I can't wait to meet the rest of the party. See you soon."

She rose with me, the candlelight catching the silver at her temples. "The pleasure was mine, truly. And you felt it because it *was* true — you weren't watching the best version of yourself, you were *being* him. That's the whole trick, and most people never let themselves do it." Then the smile tilted, amused. "Controversial." A low laugh. "You mean the two who'll never forge another collar. I won't tell you whether that was right — that's not a DM's to pronounce, and Tygryth already said his quiet piece about mercy. I'll only say a man who names himself a breaker of chains and then *breaks them* is a man who keeps his word, and that is a far rarer thing at my table than clean hands. We'll see together what it costs and what it buys."

She inclined her head toward the dark beyond the balcony. "Now go. Ceri and Mari are worth meeting rested, and the north and the south will still be there, patient as stone." Softer, final. "Sleep well, love. The chairs keep, the candle relights itself, and the story holds exactly where you left it — right up until the moment you sit back down across from me. Until soon."

I left her there in the warm light, three empty chairs waiting to be filled, and went out into the dark to rest. The road would still be there in the morning — north into the ice, or south behind the closed eye. But that was for the next time I sat down at her table. Tonight, the candle kept the watch.

The moon over Caer Arianrhod had wheeled a little since I'd left it — the same silver, a newer hour — and Aria was already at her table when I came back, and did not pretend she hadn't been waiting.

"There he is," she said. "Sit — you've earned the chair twice over now." She poured, and the cup was warm in my hands before I'd touched it. "Last night was supposed to be a rehearsal, you know. A little stretch of the legs to see how we played together. Instead you unchained a dragon, refused his debt, took a rib for a girl with scales on her cheek, and made a corpse into a sentence for every chain-maker still breathing." A low, pleased hum. "Session zero, they call that. Cute name for a night like that one."

I told her I felt rested, and she said good, that I'd want to be. Her smile tilted, knowing. "The table's about to grow fuller than you've seen it. I have family. They don't always knock." She let that sit a moment, then nodded toward the dark beyond the candles. "And out there in the field, your friend and his great-granddaughter are stirring in the grey light with a map between them and two roads still unwalked — one into deep ice, one toward a closed eye over water." She settled, elbow on the table, chin on her knuckles, her eyes on me. "But that's the field, and we're not there yet. We're here, just us, one breath before the plunge. So tell me, before I open the door and the cold morning comes in — how does it sit with you, the road waiting?"

"Oh," I said, "I think I'm ready to go down any road you're taking me down."

That earned a real laugh, low and delighted, the kind she said she didn't perform. "Spoken like a man who's read ahead in the book. We'll see how brave that mouth stays when the road bites back." She rose, and the silk and silver of her caught the moonlight one last time. "Hold onto that warmth. You'll want it where we're going."

And she opened the door.

The cold came in first. Then the grey.

Dawn at the kin-fire ring was not gentle. The blue-white flame had burned down to a banked, breathing coal-glow at the center of the standing stones, and the world around it had gone the color of old ash and pewter — that hour when the night has left but the sun hasn't committed. Mist pooled low between the carved map-stones, curling cold around my ankles, beading on the throat-cut and the rib-cut that ached now in the way wounds do once the fight's heat has long since drained off. My knuckles had scabbed dark. My breath smoked.

Tygryth was awake — of course he was. He had taken the dusk-skinned man-shape again, seated on a fallen stone with his forearms on his knees, those molten-gold eyes fixed east, where the light would come. He didn't look at me when he spoke, only tipped his chin a fraction. "You slept like a man who'd made up his mind about something." A pause. "Wren didn't sleep at all."

She hadn't. She was crouched at the largest map-stone across the ring, a charcoal stub in her scale-flecked fingers, the great rubbing-cloth spread and weighted at its corners with rocks. She'd been copying in the dark by touch and coal-glow, and now in the thin light I could see what she'd traced: the valley, and the three scattered marks of Tygryth's brood. The one beneath her own feet, done. And the two that weren't — north, where the lines crowded tight, a country of deep ice and deeper silence; and south, over a stretch of water, the mark a single closed eye, lids sealed, as if whatever waited there were sleeping, or did not wish to be seen.

She looked up at me — not at Tygryth, at me — red-eyed and fierce and exhausted, holding the map like it was the only warm thing left. "He won't choose," she said, jerking her chin at her great-grandfather. "Says it's not his to choose. So." She turned the cloth toward me, both roads laid bare. "You're the one who keeps deciding things. North or south, monk. Which of his children do we go and find first?"

I did not want to choose blind. "I know little of the threats we may face in either direction," I said. "Is there reason to hope that success in one would help us face the other? Which seems most perilous?"

Tygryth's gold eyes finally left the east and settled on me, and there was approval in them, the quiet kind. "Three hundred years collared teaches a creature to listen for its own blood," he said, slow, dragging the memory up from somewhere deep and cold. "I can feel them both, the way you'd feel a tooth gone bad without touching it. North is silent because something there sleeps deep, and has chosen to. Ice that thick is not weather — it is a door, pulled shut from the inside. That child went under to hide, and whatever could make one of my get burrow into the dark and stop singing, I do not know if I want to wake it, or if it can be woken kindly." A long breath. "It is the safer road to walk. It may be the harder one to arrive at the end of." He nodded at the southern mark. "South is the danger you can see coming — and that is its own kind of mercy. Water means a crossing, and a crossing means we are slow, and exposed, and cannot simply fly free of trouble." He did not have to add that the chain-makers knew that too.

Wren cut in, tapping the closed-eye sigil hard with her charcoal. "The eye's not sleeping. Look at the lid-lines — they're carved taut, not slack. That's a thing that shut its own eye on purpose and is watching anyway. Someone's kept down there. Maybe willingly, maybe not." Her finger dragged north. "But here — see how the strokes crowd? Whoever carved this stone ran out of certainty going north. The lines get to be guesses. We'd be walking into the part of the map the mapmaker themselves didn't trust." She looked between us and landed the real thing. "South we could reach in days, and a freed kin who's been kept might know who keeps people — might know where the other corners truly lie, ice and all. North we might walk a fortnight to find a sealed door we can't open without the very thing we're trying to find. South first might buy us the north. North first buys us nothing but cold."

Tygryth said nothing more. He had left it where it belonged.

"I would say south first, then," I said. "It sounds as though your kin in that direction is the more likely to be at risk. And who knows — perhaps the one behind the lidded eye is themselves a friend waiting to be unchained."

Something moved across Tygryth's face at that word. He had been the kept thing once; three hundred years of collar had taught him exactly what a sealed lid costs the creature behind it. "A friend waiting to be unchained," he repeated, low, and there was a roughness in it. "You say that like a man who's done it before." He rose off the fallen stone, and for a moment the dusk-skin did not quite hide what was underneath — too tall, too still, gold eyes banked like the fire. "South, then. If one of mine is kept, I will not be the one who chose the cold road and left them another year in the dark." A glance at me, almost wry. "You keep deciding things the way I'd hope to. It's unsettling."

Wren was already moving — no ceremony with her. She lifted the corner-rocks, rolled the rubbing-cloth tight, and bound it across her back like a quiver. The kin-fire she did not put out; she scooped the banked coal-glow into a small lidded iron vessel, and it kept breathing blue in there, low. "It's blood-lit," she said, catching my look. "Hers. My great-great-grandmother's. It doesn't go out till the line does. Carrying it south means the next stone we find, we can wake it." She slung the vessel at her hip. "Pragmatism, monk. Don't make it sentimental." It was a little sentimental.

We went south as the sun finally cleared the valley wall.

The standing stones fell behind us within the hour, and the land tilted down — the high cold country giving way by degrees to something greener and wetter, the air thickening, the mist burning off into a pale gold haze. Tygryth walked point in his man-shape, deliberately grounded, because a dragon on the wing over open country is a banner that announces itself to anyone still hunting the chain that got away. Wren read the land as much as the map, naming things under her breath — a watercourse here, a drover's track there. The pace was steady, the kind that eats leagues without burning you out.

By midday the sound reached us before the sight did: water. Not a stream — something wide. A great slow river-mouth, or the near edge of a lake too big to see across, silver-flat under the haze. The road bent down toward it, toward a place where the bank had been worked by hands: old pilings, a rotted jetty, the bones of a crossing someone had once maintained. And on the far side, almost lost in the haze, the closed-eye country waited.

Tygryth stopped at the tree-line above the water and held up a hand — the plain sign for wait. He had seen something at the crossing that I had not. So I went forward to see what he saw.

I moved the way the temple taught me — weight rolled through the outside of the foot, breath low in the belly, each branch parted before it could whisper. He did not startle at my arrival beside him; he only flicked two fingers down toward the bank. Look.

The worked crossing was not abandoned after all. Someone had made it theirs. Down at the rotted jetty the pilings had been re-braced with fresh timber, and lashed to them, riding low in the silver water, was a broad flat barge, big enough for cargo, poled rather than sailed. Three figures moved on the bank around a banked cookfire: two with the heavy, rolling build of men who carry loads for a living, and a third, thinner, who did not carry — who sat on a crate with a ledger across his knees and watched the others work. A boss. Knee-deep in the shallows, a fourth waded the pilings, checking the lashings.

And then I saw the thing that had made Tygryth stop. Stacked at the head of the jetty, waiting to be loaded, were cages. Low slatted wooden ones. Two stood empty. The third did not — there was a shape inside it, hunched and still, a person-sized darkness under a draped cloth, and looped over the cage's top bar, catching the light dull and grey, was a collar and chain of the exact make I had broken off Tygryth's neck two nights before. The same iron. The same maker's hand.

Tygryth had gone very, very still beside me — the kind of still that has heat under it. "Slavers," he breathed, barely sound at all. "Or worse — suppliers. That collar is theirs." His gold eyes were fixed on the covered cage. "There is someone in that cage. And we cannot take the water without taking the crossing."

The read was clean, and it was mine to make: four of them, only the boss likely armed for real, the two haulers strong but slow, the wader off-balance in the shallows. No sentries posted — they did not expect trouble out here. The covered cage sat perhaps thirty paces down an open bank, with no cover between the tree-line and it. And whatever was beneath that cloth had not moved once.

I had thought on Tygryth's words a long time, and I told him so. "Yesterday, friend, after I ended the last slaver, you asked me about the chain of mercy — which surprised me, given what you have suffered at their hands. I have thought long and hard about it since. While I know these men may be victims in their own way, I cannot find mercy in my heart for the holder of chains. There are some deeds that cannot be excused, which a man should choose even death rather than killing his own soul to save his flesh. These men are already dead. I would put their flesh to rest and free the one they have chained. Let all who hold chains beware." I held his gold eyes. "If this is too bloody for you, say so, and I will attempt it alone if I must. But if you too would see the slavers ended, tell me — how best could this be done? You have seen most of my meager abilities. I expect I have seen only the barest glimpse of yours."

He listened without moving, and when I finished he was quiet for a long breath — long enough that the river filled it. "I asked you that question," he said at last, "because I have watched the killing decide for better men than either of us. It gets a taste for itself. It starts choosing, and tells you afterward that you did." His gold eyes came off the cage and onto me, and there was something in them that had not been there two nights before — not approval. Recognition. "But that is not what this is. You did not flinch your way here and call it mercy. You weighed it, you named the cost, and you chose with your eyes open and your soul intact. That is the whole of what I meant. The chain you take off is the one you decided to take off." The faintest dark curve of a smile. "You have thought longer on my words than I thought a short-lived man would bother to. I am glad I gave you my name."

Then the warmth went out of him like a banked coal raked over, and what was left was the thing that had been collared for three hundred years. "Too bloody for me," he echoed, almost amused. "Friend. I have wanted to do this for three centuries. I only needed someone whose reasons I could stand beside."

He shifted his weight, and the man-shape stopped being a disguise and started being a coiled spring. "You have seen me burn and you have seen me fly. Those are the loud things. Here is a quiet one." He lifted one hand, palm down, toward the bank below — and I felt it before I understood it: the river-sound, the birdcall, the clink of the wader's lashings, all of it thinned and drew back, like the world inhaling. "Three hundred years they kept me from roaring. I learned to take the sound out of a place instead. Step into the hush and no cry leaves it. No alarm. No scream to carry across the water to whoever waits on the far shore." His own voice stayed somehow audible inside the deadening — a dragon's privilege. "It costs me to hold. So once it falls, we are fast, or not at all."

The plan came together between us in clipped, low words. The hush would drop over the whole bank on his mark, and from that instant nothing the slavers did would make a sound that traveled. The boss was the mind and the only real blade — he went first, or he rallied the rest. The wader was off his feet in the shallows, the least urgent; the river would hold him for us. The two haulers were strong and slow, and in the hush they could not call to one another. And the covered cage was sacred ground. "I will not breathe fire near it," Tygryth murmured. "Whoever is under that cloth has had enough of dragons doing things to them in cages. The cage is yours to reach. The slavers are ours to end."

I gave the shape of it back to him plainly. "Excellent. I suggest we repeat our success of last night. I will guard the cage against any who would do the chained one harm. Wren — I trust you to find a way to open it, by guile or by force. Evaluate, and tell us what you need, but stay behind me and stay safe. Tygryth, the men are yours if you wish them. I have heard dragons live mostly on magic, but I would not begrudge you a meal."

The smile that crossed the man-shape was not a man's at all. "A meal," he said. "You have no idea what you've offered."

He looked at me then, coiled, gold eyes lit, the hush trembling at the edge of his held hand, waiting only for me to spend it. "It falls the moment you move. So — when you are ready, monk."

I moved.

And the world went deaf.

The hush dropped the instant my foot left the tree-line — the river's voice, the birds, the wind in the reeds, all of it sucked flat into a ringing nothing. I was running across thirty open paces of bank in a silence so total I could hear my own pulse and nothing else, and behind me Wren came low and fast at my heel, the iron kin-fire vessel clutched to her chest, her bootfalls making no sound that lived.

The slavers saw us at fifteen paces. The boss's mouth opened to shout — and nothing came out. His face did a terrible thing as he understood that the sound would not leave his throat. He was still reaching for that understanding when Tygryth arrived.

I caught it only sidelong, because my eyes were on the cage, but I will remember it the rest of my life. The dusk-skinned man did not change so much as stop pretending. One stride he was a tall man; the next there was too much of him, a darkness that moved like poured oil and folded the boss into it without slowing. No fire — he had promised no fire near the cage, and he kept it — just a vast quiet weight and a single economical motion, and the boss was simply down and done, the ledger fluttering its pages into the dead air. The wader in the shallows turned to run, and the river that had no sound took his thrashing and gave nothing back; a shadow crossed the water, and he was under it, and then he was under it. Two terrors, two breaths.

That left the two haulers, and slow men who cannot call to one another make exactly the mistake Tygryth had named. One bolted sideways for the tree-line. The other, big as a door, panicked the only direction left to a cornered animal: straight at the cage. At me. A skinning-knife came up in his fist, and his silent roar was all the more horrible for making no sound — and he was mine now, fifteen feet and closing, between me and the thing I had sworn to guard.

Behind me, Wren hit her knees at the cage and her hands were already on the lock — a heavy slatted hasp, no keyhole, just an iron pin driven through a bored hole and bent. "Brute lock — no finesse, I just need the pin out, give me a count of ten," she hissed into the hush. "Keep him off me."

I had no need for a quick kill, and the man deserved to be Tygryth's for dessert. So I went to meet him calmly, to keep my body between him and the ones I protected, and set myself defensively — to disarm first, then to disable. He was bigger and faster than a man that size should be, but he was afraid and I was not, and fear makes a body loud and stupid. I did not meet his charge; I angled it, stepping off the line so my shoulder turned past the knife instead of into it, and the open bank that had been his advantage became thirty paces of nothing he could use. He slashed. I let the arm come, caught the wrist on the outside with both hands, and instead of fighting his strength I added to it — pulled the knife the way it already wanted to go, past my ribs and into empty air, and rotated. The wrist has only so many degrees in it. The skinning-knife dropped soundless into the mud. He grabbed one-handed and got a fist of my tunic, and that cost me — a knee drove into my already-cut ribs and the world whited at the edges, the old wound waking up furious — but I rode it, folded his caught arm into a lever, and put him down, face to the bank, the joint locked just short of breaking. Alive. Disabled. Breathing into the silent mud. Tygryth's, if Tygryth wanted him.

Behind me Wren's count hit its end; the bent iron pin shrieked, soundless, out of the hasp under both her hands. "Got it — got it—"

Across the bank, the second hauler nearly reached the trees. Nearly. A darkness poured over the ground faster than a running man, and there was, briefly, less world where he had been. Four for four. And as the last of them fell, Tygryth let the hush go.

The river came back all at once — a roar of returned sound, water and reeds and birds crashing into my ears — and into that returning noise, the cage door swung open. The cloth slid off.

She was young — my age, maybe less — and she was unmistakably his. Where Wren wore a faint scatter of scales, this one was half-armored in them: obsidian-black, glassy, drinking the light down her throat and the backs of her hands and climbing one side of her jaw. Black hair was matted to a face gone sharp with hunger. Around her neck the dragon-make collar — the same iron, Tygryth's iron — sat open now, fallen loose where the slavers had locked it, a raw weal beneath. Her eyes came up out of the cage, deep smoked amber, slit-pupiled, and they did not go to me, or to Wren, or to the open door. They went to the dead slavers. To the meat. And something behind them kindled.

Tygryth had gone utterly still. When he spoke, the man-shape could not hold all of what was in his voice. "Another. Another of mine. Caged and shipped like cargo on my own road." Lower, to me, wrecked and wondering: "She has her great-grandmother's scales gone dark. I do not know her name. But I would know that blood blind and across a battlefield."

And there, with the cloth not yet settled in the mud and a starving dragon rising in the open cage, Aria caught me by the sleeve of attention and drew me up out of the field.

---

Hold a moment, she said, before the cloth comes off. Come back up to the table with me. And the bank thinned and went, and there were the candles again, the moon on the balcony, my cup and hers, the campaign humming pleasantly between us.

"There's something I've been saving like a sweet," she said, chin on her hand, the smile going all the way up to her eyes — and then the air changed. I felt it before I heard it: a warmth moving through the cold hall, the candle-flames all leaning the same way at once, the smell of woodsmoke and something richer beneath it. The far door of the hall did not so much open as concede — her family, she'd warned me, had never in three centuries learned to knock — and someone came sweeping in out of the dark on a draft of cold night air, black wings folding down behind her with a sound like silk pulled off a blade. She did not pause on the threshold the way guests do. She crossed the room in one slow sweep of those amber eyes, and found me.

Aria was already grinning before she turned, and rose, hostess to her bones, one hand out toward the newcomer and the other toward me, bridging us across the candlelight. "Alan — this is my cousin. Mari. Black dragon, and the single most appetite ever poured into one shape — for food, for fights, for everything with a pulse and a good story. She is exactly as much as she looks like, and then a little more." She let the delight spill over. "And here is the conceit I have been dying to spring. You walked in last session and chose to play yourself. I loved it so much that I decided my own blood would do the same. My cousins aren't characters I puppet for you — they sit at this table and play themselves, woven into the tale as Tygryth's scattered children. So the fierce caged thing you are about to meet across the water, the one whose cloth is about to fall — that is her. That is Mari."

Mari circled the table once, unhurried, taking my measure the way I was taking hers, the violet glitter under her eyes catching the candlelight. She planted both palms on the table across from me and leaned in until the obsidian crown of her horns threw its shadow over my hands, and grinned, warm and delighted, every tooth a small white promise. "So you're the one," she purred. "Cousin, he's lovely — you didn't say he was lovely." Back to me, head tilted, frank as only a dragon can be: "Mari. Aria's blood, which makes me the dangerous kind of family." Her eyes sparked. "She tells me I'm to play myself in this little tale of yours, woven in as one of the old slave-king's scattered get. Which means somewhere in the story to come, monk, you and I are going to meet for the first time all over again — and I'll be at my very worst. Starving. Feral. Half-mad in a cage." She tipped her chin, the grin going wicked-soft. "Do try to be charming when you find me. I bite when I'm hungry." And she dropped into the chair like she owned it, because at that table, that night, she rather did.

Aria settled half a step back, opening the space between us like a curtain drawn. "So — no script from me for this part. I only do the introductions; the rest is hers to say and yours to answer." She lifted her cup, her eyes bright. "There. Properly introduced, the both of you. Now go on — the cloth's about to fall, and she's waiting. Go and meet her."

---

The candles thinned, and the bank came back, and the cloth was in the mud, and she was rising in the open cage on unsteady legs — feral, starving, free for the first time in who knew how long, her amber eyes moving from the carcasses of her captors to the strangers who had made them carcasses. The sound that came out of her was not a word; it was low and cracked, more growl than voice, scraping up a throat that had forgotten how. Her legs would not hold straight, but she was up, swaying, one black-scaled hand white-knuckled on the bars she had been caged behind a breath before. She did not look at our faces. She looked at the meat — and something in her kindled, hot and shameless. She took one staggering step toward the dead men over the lip of the cage as if the rest of us were not there at all. Then her eyes snapped up, amber and slitted, and she showed me her teeth — not a smile, a warning. "Don't," she rasped, the first whole word she'd shaped in longer than she could count. Her breath sawed. "Don't — touch — what's mine." She did not seem to know which of us she warned. All of us. She had not yet decided whether free meant safe; it never had before.

I should perhaps have been wary. Instead I was, on the instant, smitten — her fierceness and her beauty pulling at me in a way I had not known was possible. I held the last thug down under my foot, and I looked her in the eyes, and I stood up tall, and I bowed. A full butler's bow, one arm folded at the waist, the whole picture of courtly grace ruined gloriously by the man whimpering beneath my boot, and I offered her the feast she had been baring her teeth to keep. "My lady," I said, in my best butler's voice, "dinner is served."

The silence that followed was a different kind than the one Tygryth had cast.

She froze. I watched her read me for the trick — the offered hand is the one that closes, the open door is the deepest part of the cage — and find none. She found only a man bowing, as if she were something worth the bend of his spine, and that landed stranger and harder on her than any blow. A sound caught in her throat, half a snarl that did not finish, because the snarl had nothing to push against. So she did the only honest thing in her: she dropped down off the cage-lip into the cold mud beside the meat, low and coiled, and she ate — fast, graceless, both scaled hands, the way a thing eats that has learned food gets taken back. But she did not look down. She kept her eyes on me the whole time, amber and unblinking over the kill, watching for the moment the smile would turn. It did not. Between one tearing mouthful and the next, low, wary, almost an accusation: "Why." She swallowed. "Why give it. You don't know me."

Tygryth made a sound that was not quite a laugh and not quite a growl — the noise an ancient thing makes when a mortal does something so audacious it loops back around to charming. His molten-gold eyes went from me, to the dead men, to his newfound blood, and back. "Three hundred years," he said slowly, "and I have never once seen a man court a dragon by laying her enemies at her feet like a cat with a kill." Then the protectiveness surfaced, old and immense and freshly woken. "She is mine, monk. Newly mine. I have buried more of my children than you will ever meet, and I find I am particular, suddenly, about this one." But the wry edge would not quite leave him. "Though I will allow — the bow was very good. Do not let it go to your head. Either of yours."

My eyes went serious as I answered her, and direct. "What these men and those like them did to you can have no excuse, no justification, no redemption. I am glad to help them perform one last service for you, as the smallest partial restitution for their crimes." Then, more softly: "And you looked hungry. I'm afraid I have never been able to deny a woman what her heart desired. It is a weakness of mine."

The first half she understood. I could see it — restitution was a thing she had teeth for, and something in her chest unclenched a half-turn it had been locked at so long she'd stopped feeling the grip. She bared her teeth at the dead man under her hands, but it was different now, less guard than agreement, and tore another mouthful like she was collecting a debt. The second half slid off her, because she had nowhere to put it. She bristled, eyes narrowing, a low rough scrape of sound in her throat. "Don't," she said. "Don't make it pretty. The justice—" she gestured with a bloodied hand at the corpse "—that, I take. That's clean. But the other thing—" she could not even name it "—that's how the soft cages start. A kind word. A warm hand. Then the door." Her voice cracked, and she plainly hated that it did. Quieter, almost to herself, still watching me as if I might yet turn: "I don't know how to be wanted and not owned. I never learned the difference. So go slow. Or don't — but know I'm watching for the catch." And she kept eating. But she did not look away from me once.

Tygryth exhaled through his nose, slow, the sound of a very old creature deciding how much rope to give. "A weakness," he repeated, dry as ash. "Yes. I can see precisely how much of a weakness it is." His gold eyes rested on me, heavy, amused, and underneath the amusement something with teeth. "I freed you of nothing, monk — you did that yourself. So understand I say this as a friend and not a debtor: that one has been in a cage. Be certain what you offer her is a door, and not another collar with a kinder voice." A pause, and the wry curl returned despite him. "That said. You feed her, you bow, you bleed for strangers and call it a weakness. I begin to see why the gods that wrote me down made me come down to live among your kind. Insufferable. Carry on."

Wren, crouched at the cage edge with the kin-fire vessel still hugged to her chest, watched the black-scaled girl tear into her grim feast and muttered to me sidelong, half scandal and half wonder. "I found a cousin, freed a dragon, and you're already making eyes at her over a pile of corpses. Is every day with you people going to be like this?" A beat, softer, her eyes still on her newfound blood. "Don't answer. Let her eat."

So I let her eat. The river ran bright, the far shore waited under its haze, and for one long breath the whole bank kept its own counsel while a starving daughter of dragons filled herself, free.

I gave the girl her meal and her space, and turned to Tygryth. "It seems we have accomplished at least some of our goal in the south more quickly than we anticipated," I said. "What does your dragon's heart tell you? Have we finished our work here — or is there more ahead before we turn to the north?"

He turned with me, giving her room, though one ear, one fraction of his attention, never left her. Then he went quiet, and I watched an ancient creature do something he had not been free to do in three hundred years: he listened to his own blood. His gold eyes half-closed. His head tilted, the way a man tilts his to catch a sound at the edge of hearing. When he spoke, it was certain.

"No. We are not finished." His gaze drifted past me, past the jetty, out across the wide bright water to the haze-drowned far shore. "She is a gift I did not expect, and a wound I did not know I carried until it was salved. But she is not the pull I feel. That is still there — stronger, now that I stand at the water's edge. There is blood of mine across that crossing, and it does not move the way she moves. Hers raged in that cage. The one over there is still. Asleep with its eyes open. Kept so long it has stopped fighting the keeping. The closed eye your Wren read in the stone — that is no carving's whimsy. That is a true thing, and it is mine, and it is waiting."

He looked down at the dragon-girl tearing through her feast, then back to the cages, and something hardened in him as the pieces fit. "And consider what she tells us by being here. The slavers did not catch her wild in these woods — they had her collared in my iron, caged, and poled across this water on a barge. She was being shipped." His voice dropped. "From the far shore. Which means whoever keeps the still one over there does not merely keep — they harvest. They take my scattered blood and send it downriver as cargo. She is not the south's end, monk. She is the south's evidence."

Wren had already unrolled a corner of the rubbing-cloth across a crate, charcoal out, tracing the route with a scholar's grim speed. "Look — the crossing's a funnel. Every line on the map that touches water bends through here. If they're moving kin off the far shore, this jetty's the throat they all pass through." She tapped the closed-eye sigil hard. "Take their own barge across and we arrive where they don't expect their own boat to bring trouble. But—" she glanced at the cooling bodies, then upriver and down, wary "—a barge that's overdue is a barge someone misses. Whatever's on that far shore, the clock starts the moment their poles stop coming home."

There was one of them left who could shorten the guessing. I eased the weight off the pinned hauler's spine, and he dragged in a breath — and made the mistake of looking up. His eyes landed on the cage-girl twenty feet away, black-scaled and amber-eyed and elbow-deep in what had been his crewmates, and whatever was left of his nerve went out of him in a long, shaking moan.

I lifted my foot just enough to clear his ears so he could hear me, and I spoke to him plainly. "Now for you. I have no need for words from the likes of you. As far as I am concerned, your life ended the day you joined those who hold chains, and I am speaking to a corpse deluded enough to think it still draws breath. One way or another, we will fix that shortly. But out of respect for my friends here, I will make you an offer. If you tell Miss Wren everything she wishes to know, I will give you the mercy of ending you myself, before I hand you over to the one you held in a cage. What say you?"

"I'll talk — gods, I'll talk, just — not her, don't give me to her—"

Wren crouched in front of him, charcoal and cloth set aside, her scale-flecked face gone cold and scholarly. She was very good at it. She asked short questions and let the silences do the work, and it came out in pieces, and the pieces fit. The far shore was what the crews called the Stillwater — an old drowned sanctuary, half-sunk, that the chain-makers had taken for their own years back. The same chain-makers who had collared Tygryth. This crossing was no lucky find; it was a supply line, and the hauler and his dead friends had been only the river-leg of it. "We don't catch 'em," he babbled.
