"Rangers do that — inland, the wild ones, the ones with the scales. We just pole 'em downriver to market once they're collared and broke. That's all I do, I swear it, I just pole the boat—"

Wren's voice could have cut glass. "The collars. Where does the iron come from?"

He went grey, because here was the thing they did not say aloud. "The Well." He would not look at the far shore. "There's one they keep. Down in the Stillwater, under the old eye-mark. Been there longer than any of us — old, big, quiet. Don't fight no more, don't hardly move. The Warden bleeds it. That's where the iron gets its bite, see — they quench the collars in dragon's blood, that's why the chains hold what they hold. The Well's the wellspring. They'd never kill it. It's worth more bled slow than dead."

I felt Tygryth go to stone behind me. The still one. His blood. Kept alive three centuries to be drained drop by drop into the very chains they put on the rest of his line.

Wren held her voice flat by sheer will and drove for the part that mattered. "We're taking your barge across. You're going to tell me how to dock without a fight. How many. What signal."

He gave it all up. The barge ran the crossing at dusk — always dusk, never full dark, so the dock-watch could see the hull. On approach you hung a hooded blue lantern off the bow-hook; it was stowed under the steering-bench, he said, his voice cracking. The dock answered with two flashes; you answered with one, then shipped the poles. Cargo stayed covered until the Warden's man had tallied it — nobody uncovered cargo on the water, it was how the wild ones were kept calm. The dock itself was lightly held: three, maybe four, because who attacks a harvest from its own river? But inland, up in the drowned shrine, there was the Warden, a handful of rangers between hunts, and the cage-hands. "A dozen, fifteen, more when a hunt's in," he whispered. "But the dock — the dock's just us. Was just us."

Wren sat back on her heels, pale, the route suddenly real on the cloth before her — the funnel, the dusk crossing, the blue lantern, the closed eye, the Well beneath it. "It's enough," she said quietly, to Tygryth and me both. "We can wear their own skin right up to the dock. After that it's a knife-fight in a sunken temple against people who make chains for a living." She swallowed. "To free something that's forgotten it wants to be free."

He had talked, and he had kept his half. The offer had been simple: he talks, and I end him clean before the dragon-girl can. So I kept mine. I squatted and braced my hands on either side of his thick neck and twisted. He was stronger than most, but the correct application of force is enough, and his spine went. He died without pain, as I had promised — which was more than he deserved. "More than he deserved," I murmured, and rose, and wiped my hands on my ruined tunic, and that was the end of him.

For a moment no one spoke. The river filled the silence.

Tygryth watched the body settle, and watched me, and something moved in those molten eyes that was older and heavier than the fight that had come before. When he spoke it was low, and it was only for me. "You gave your word to a dead man." Not a question. "A creature with nothing left to offer you, nothing to threaten you with, no one to hold you to it — and you kept it to the letter anyway. Talk, and a clean death before the worse one. He talked. You gave it clean." He was quiet a beat. "Three hundred years I was bled on other men's promises. We will free you. We will not hurt the others. Tell us and it ends. Every one of them a lie, paid out in iron." His gaze did not leave me. "You did not have to keep that one, monk. No one living would have known. I would not have known. That is precisely why it matters that you did." A slow breath. "Mercy is a chain you wear by choice. Today I watched you choose it with your eyes open and your hands steady — and that is a different thing entirely from the killing choosing for you. I think I begin to trust the man at the other end of it."

Wren said nothing for a while. She rolled the rubbing-cloth, tied off the kin-fire vessel at her hip, and only as she straightened did she let it out, quiet. "My great-great-grandmother lit a fire with her own blood, so her line would have something warm to come home to. These people light iron with it." Her jaw set. "Let's go put their lantern on their boat, and sail it down their own throat."

Behind me the dragon-daughter had eaten her fill; the bank was quiet now but for the water. The barge waited at the jetty, broad and patient, the hooded blue lantern stowed beneath its bench. Dusk was hours off yet — time to bind my wounds, time for the freed one to find her feet, time to become, for one crossing, the very thing we had been killing. The closed eye waited across the bright water, sleeping and watching and kept. And we turned, together now and one larger than we had been at dawn, toward the boat.

The black-scaled girl ate apart from us, and I left her to it; I did not want to crowd a creature still deciding whether free meant safe. So I went to Tygryth instead, and sat, and asked him for the one thing no one in three hundred years had thought to.

"Friend," I said, "I know I am not yet strong enough to truly stand at your side in what is coming. You have seen me fight. You have lived long and learned much. Is there anything you could teach me, while we prepare for the next step of the road?"

Something shifted in the ancient face — surprised, in a way three centuries rarely allow. He glanced once at the freed girl finding her feet apart from us, and marked that I had given her the room, and then he settled onto the fallen piling and gestured me down across from him.

"In three centuries no short-lived thing has ever asked me to teach it," he said. "They ask me to fight for them, to fly them somewhere, to frighten someone. You ask to be more than you are." A slow nod. "Your creed. The one thing they cannot collar is the self you make. Yes. I can teach to that." He held up one hand — the same hand that had pulled the sound out of the world. "You think the hush is a dragon's trick, beyond you. It is not — not the root of it. The root is subtraction. When I take the sound from a place, first I take it from myself — my own breath, my own heart-drum, the roar of my own wanting. Only when I am quiet inside can I feel what the world is doing outside." His gold eyes held mine. "You already do a sliver of this. That hauler — you did not watch the knife. You felt where it was already going, and stepped off the line before it arrived. You read his intent in the breath before the strike. You did it by instinct. I will teach you to do it by will."

He laid out the lesson plainly: sit, breathe low into the belly, and put down the noise inside one strand at a time — the ache in the ribs, the drum of the heart, and loudest of all the wanting, the part braced for the next fight. Quiet all three, he said, and the world gets louder; intent has a texture, and it arrives a half-breath before motion does, and a half-breath is everything. "It will not come today," he said. "It comes in years. But the first sitting is the first stone, and we have hours before dusk." Across the bank Wren wrestled the blue lantern out from under the steering-bench and threw over her shoulder, dry, "Oh, good — meditation. I'll just rig the boat that sails us into a chain-maker temple all by myself, shall I?" There was no real bite in it. She left us to it.

So I sat, and I went straight past the first three steps. I had long known how to take the sound out of myself — to still all noise and rope my breath to my heartbeat; that part of his discipline I had carried since the temple. So I reached past it, outward, for the thing I had felt when he stilled not only himself but the world. He had said I could do the same. I trusted him. I tried to replicate it, even the smallest part.

And I reached for the wrong thing, and almost touched it anyway.

I could not take the sound from the world — I understood later I was never going to; the hush is wrung from a muscle no human body owns. But in that perfect inner quiet I found the place where he gripped it. My awareness brushed a seam in the world, a cold smooth edge, the handle of a door far too large for my hand. I could not pull it open. But for one heartbeat I leaned my weight on it — and the river dropped a half-tone, just around me, just for that breath, a small soft circle an arm's span wide where the reeds went faint and the water pulled back and my own silent heartbeat was the loudest thing left. Then it snapped shut, and the cost landed all at once: a bright spike behind my eyes, a thread of warmth at my nose.

When I opened my eyes, Tygryth's were wide, the molten gold of them lit with something I had not seen on him before. Not pride. Closer to alarm. "Stop. Stop there." His hand came up, gentle, halting. "You felt the seam." It was not a question. "Three hundred years, monk. It took me the better part of a century behind a collar to find the edge of that door, with a dragon's body screaming at me to. You found it in a single sitting and leaned your whole weight on it with a borrowed hand. There is blood on your lip. That is the door telling you it is too heavy. Push it the way you just tried and you will tear something in yourself that does not grow back." The alarm cooled into a teacher's care, and something graver underneath. "So hear the lesson change. You are not built to take the sound. But you have proved you can feel the seam — and feeling is the half that matters in a fight. You reached for my power and brushed my senses instead, and the senses are yours to keep, safely, for as long as you train them." A dark, slow almost-smile. "I offered to teach you a stone a year. You picked up three before the river warmed your blood. I will be honest, friend — you frighten me a little. Keep the sensing. Leave the door to me. Now wipe your face, and this time reach only to listen — not to push."

I wiped my lip, and breathed, and understood. "Thank you for the concern and the guidance," I said. "I think I follow. But it would be easier with something to sense — something to stand in for the threats I'll need to find later." I turned and called across the bank to the girl with the black scales, with a smile. "My lady — would you care to amuse yourself by throwing pebbles at me while I meditate? I would count it a favor."

She was crouched with her back to the cage she'd climbed out of, a flat river-stone already turning over and over in her scaled fingers. Her head tilted, amber eyes narrowing, and something that was not quite a smile pulled at the corner of her mouth. "You'll regret asking," she told me, low and rough. "I don't miss." The first pebble was already gone — a lazy underhand flick, no real venom in it, a test throw aimed to clip my shoulder.

I closed my eyes and let it come. And I felt it — not the stone, the intent: a small wrongness plucking at the edge of my stilled awareness, a pull off to my left a half-second before it arrived. I felt it, and could not place it fast enough; my mind reached toward it, grabbed for it, tried to hunt it down — and the stone clipped my shoulder, a clean light tap, exactly where she'd aimed. But my shoulder had already begun to turn. A finger's width. A heartbeat late, yet unmistakably moving — my body answering a warning my mind hadn't finished reading.

Tygryth made a low pleased sound. "There. You felt it — and then you chased it, and the chasing is what cost you the half-breath. This is the hardest turn for a fighting man: do less. Do not hunt the threat. Let it arrive. Sit like a still pool and let its wrongness fall into you as a ripple. Your body already trusts the sense more than your mind does. Now get your loud, clever mind out of its way."

"I nod," I said, and stilled myself again, eyes closed, and let it come.

This time I did not chase. This time I was a still pool with my eyes shut — and so the lie never reached me, because the lie was for the eyes. Two stones left her hands. To a watching man the high one would have been the whole world: slow, bright, arcing, here it comes, catch it. But I was not watching. In the quiet the high stone arrived almost weightless, a pretty thing with no venom behind it, a ripple so faint it barely stirred the pool. It carried no meaning. The low one screamed — off her knuckles, sidearm, blind-side, aimed at the seam of my ribs, a hard dark ripple of real intent, the only honest thing she threw. I felt it a half-breath early, low and to the right, and for once my clever mind stayed out of the way; my forearm was already dropping across my body, and the rib-cracker met the meat of my arm with a flat crack and skipped off into the reeds. The pretty stone sailed past my unmoved head and plopped into the river, ignored. I never opened my eyes.

For a moment there was only the river and her rough, surprised laugh hanging in the gold air. "Now we're playing," she breathed.

Tygryth took a breath before he trusted his voice. "Do you understand what you just did? She lied to you with the bright stone, the way every real enemy will. And it did nothing, because you were not watching her hand — you were feeling her intent. Here is the whole secret, and you found it yourself: a feint is a lie the eye can be told, but it is a lie the sense cannot, because the real blow still has to mean it. The killing stroke always carries weight the decoy does not. The eye sees two threats. The stillness hears only the one that means to land." He shook his head slowly. "I could lie to your eyes all day. I do not think I could lie to that." A glance at his feral kin, crouched and grinning with a third stone already in her fingers, and something rueful and warm crossed the dusk-dark face. "And it seems my blood has decided she likes you. Gods help us both."

This time I stayed still with my eyes closed, but resolved that if I caught the stone I would send it back to her. And she did something I would only understand after. She rocked up onto her knees and picked the throw clean and slow and announced — a straight true arc, no feint beneath it, no second truth hiding behind the first. "This one's true," she told me, low, and I heard that she meant more than the stone. "No catch in it." The pebble left her fingers. "See if you can tell the difference now — between the stone that wants to hurt you, and the one that just wants to be caught."

It fell into my stillness with no lie laid over it — one clean ripple, single and true, arriving exactly where the sense said it would and exactly when. The rib-cracker had screamed; this one did not scream at all. It came in soft, unhurried, almost asking, a ripple shaped less like a threat than like an open hand. My eyes stayed closed. My hand rose on its own — not a block, not the hard tuck of a forearm, but my palm turning up and open into the dusk-gold air — and the stone settled into it as if it had been thrown for no other reason. My fingers closed. Caught. It was the first thing all evening that did not feel like training. It felt like an answer.

I had meant to throw it back. I did not. I opened my eyes and found hers already on me, and instead of returning the stone I closed my hand around it and tucked it away into my pocket. "Thank you, my lady, for assisting me in this," I said, and meant every word of it. "I hope you enjoyed it as much as I did — and I will treasure your gift."

Something in her face came undone before she could stop it. She looked away fast, down at her own scaled hands, and when her voice came it was rougher than she wanted, reaching for gruffness like the only armor she had left. "It's a rock, monk. The river's full of them." But she could not make it land mean. It came out wrecked and small, and she did not take it back.

And then — because there were dead men waiting across the water who needed reminding what they had become, and I told her so as I turned toward the boat — I felt her not let me go the way the cage had taught her to. She got up. Legs steadier than they had been an hour before, blood and river-mud drying on her hands, and she fell in beside me — not behind, not at heel, but at my side, close enough that her shoulder could brush my arm. She did not ask if she was allowed. "Where you're going," she said, low, the gruff gone now, just bare and certain underneath, "there's more of them. More of the men who make cages. I'm coming." A breath, and then the truth slipped out, quieter, the first thing she had ever chosen to belong to. "Not for you. For the ones still in the dark, waiting for someone to take the cloth off. Somebody should have come for me sooner." Her jaw set. "So I'll go be the somebody." And she looked at me sidelong, the ghost of the grin coming back, feral and alive. "Try to keep up."

Tygryth had gone very still, and when he looked at her there were three centuries behind his eyes. "For three hundred years I have watched my blood be taken into the dark," he said, for her alone. "I have never once watched it walk in on its own feet to bring someone out." He inclined his head to her — not a grandfather to a child, but one dragon to another, the deepest courtesy his kind owns. "That is the thing they could never collar." Then, sidelong to me, dry as old stone, reassembling himself: "You have set something loose in my blood, monk. I have not decided whether to thank you or fear you. Likely both."

And then it was time, and the four of us went down to the water as the last gold drained out of the west.

Wren came down from the map-stones, the kin-fire vessel breathing blue at her hip, the rubbing-cloth bound across her back. Tygryth kept the dusk-man shape — no dragon on the wing tonight, not into a chain-maker's house. The slavers' broad flat barge waited at the rotted jetty, poles racked, and Wren ducked under the steering-bench and came up with the hooded blue lantern, exactly where the dead man had sworn it would be. She turned it over in her hands and recited it like a grim catechism. "Two flashes off the far dock. We answer with one. Ship the poles. Cargo stays covered till their man tallies it — nobody uncovers the boat on the water." She looked up at the three of us. "Three, maybe four on the dock. The Warden and his rangers are inland, up in the drowned shrine. And the still one's under the eye-mark, where they've bled it three hundred years to put the bite in their iron." A hard swallow. "We take their own boat, fly their own light, and sail it straight down their throat."

I struck the lantern. The blue flame caught on the third try, and it was not a normal fire: it burned cold and low and wrong, a sick lovely color that threw no warmth, the same blue as the kin-fire at Wren's hip but bled of everything kind. I understood, looking at it, that this lantern had been quenched in the same well their iron was. I hooded it, unhooded it, learned its little shutter in the dark, and then Tygryth set the pole to the mud and pushed, and the jetty slid away behind us, and there was only black water.

The crossing was long, and silent, and the worst part of the night.

The barge moved slow — it had to; a barge that hurries is a barge that's afraid, and afraid is a thing watchers notice. So we glided. The Stillwater's careless lights sat low across the water and did not seem to come closer for a long while, and then all at once they did, resolving out of the dark into torch-smear and the bones of a landing, pilings and a half-drowned stone quay, and above it, climbing into the starlight, the broken shoulder of something vast and sunken. A sanctuary, once. I could feel it the way I had only just learned to feel things, eyes half-lidded — a great low wrongness sitting over the whole far shore, and under it, fainter and deeper, a single quiet ache, slow as a tired heartbeat, that I somehow knew without being told was the thing they kept. It did not scream. It had forgotten how. It only ached, down under the closed stone eye, patient as drowning.

The black-scaled girl felt it too. I sensed her go rigid at my shoulder, the grin gone flat, a low sound swallowed in her throat. Her blood. Wren sank lower over the cargo-shape we'd arranged to look right, the kin-fire vessel pressed to her chest, knuckles white. Tygryth poled, even and unhurried, wearing a dead trade like a borrowed coat, and only the set of his jaw said what it cost him to bring his own calm face into the house that had bled his children.

A hundred yards out, the far dock noticed us. A lantern lifted on the quay and flashed — once, twice — the agreed count, lazy, expecting nothing. Tygryth's hand moved to the hooded blue flame and answered. Once. A single shuttered blink across the black water. A pause that lasted a small forever. Then the dock-lantern dipped — accepted, bored — and a voice carried thin across the water, not alarmed, just routine. "Late. Bring it in." The poles shipped. The barge glided the last stretch on its own dark momentum, and now I could count them: three on the quay, a fourth slouched by a brazier further up, loose and unarmored, a crew that had done this a thousand times and never once been the ones in danger. No rangers in sight. The hull kissed the stone quay with a soft grinding nudge, and a tally-man stepped to the edge above us, lantern in one hand and a tally-stick in the other, already bending to count the covered cargo — close enough that I could see the boredom on his face, close enough to smell the smoke on him, close enough to touch.

He leaned in over the covered shape. He reached for the cloth.

I stepped up behind him, set my hands to either side of his head, and twisted, and his neck broke with a small wet crack, and he folded without a sound, the cloth still pinched in his dead fingers. That was the signal to act.

The dock came apart in the space of four breaths.

Tygryth poured the hush out the instant the body dropped. The world went deaf around the quay the way it had at the river — the lap of the water gone, the brazier's crackle gone, a bubble of pure silence thrown over the landing — and into that silence he stopped pretending to be a man. The dusk-shape unfolded into pouring dark, and the two slavers nearest the rail died before their bored faces had finished changing, taken into the black weight of him and simply not there anymore. No shout. No splash. The hush ate it all.

The black-scaled girl was over the gunwale a half-beat behind me, and she went for the third — a cage-hand with the heavy keys still hanging at his belt, a maker of the very locks she had worn that morning. Her hand found his mouth first, palm clamped hard over the shout before it could form, and the obsidian came up her arm in a fast black tide, fingers going to claw; she pulled his head back into her shoulder, gentle as a lover, and opened his throat with the other hand. One clean rake. No cry — she drank the sound right out of his mouth with her palm and lowered him quiet onto the boards so even his falling would not tell on us. For a breath she crouched over him in the dark, and I felt the cold thing in her settle into something terribly like rightness. Under her breath, not for him, just for the dark and the ones still bleeding under the stone: "One."

Wren did the unglamorous, vital thing: off the barge and onto the quay with the bow-line, lashing the hull fast so it could not drift loose and strand us, the kin-fire vessel slung tight to her back, her eyes snapping across the dock for exactly the thing that goes wrong.

And it nearly did. The fourth man, the slouched one up-dock by the brazier, stood just far enough up the stone that the edge of the hush only lapped at him. He felt the wrongness before he understood it — the night gone suddenly, impossibly quiet, his crewmates not where they had been. He could not shout; the hush smothered it to a strangled rasp. But he wheeled and lunged, not for a weapon, for the thing every dock like this keeps: a hung iron bar on a chain by the brazier, the alarm, one good strike from waking the whole drowned shrine above. His hand closed on it. He swung it at the hanging plate — and the darkness that was Tygryth was already there, faster than a falling man, and took him off his feet a hair too late. The iron grazed the plate. Not a full strike. A glancing kiss of metal on metal — and at the very lip of the hush, where the silence frayed thin, it let out one dull, half-swallowed note. A single low clang, there and gone, muffled like a bell heard underwater.

Then the man was gone into the dark with the others, and it was over, and Tygryth let the hush fall. Sound rushed back — water, brazier, my own breath. The dock was ours. Four down, none standing, the barge lashed, the cold blue lantern still burning its sick light over a quay gone suddenly, completely still.

But that one note hung in all our minds. Tygryth re-formed the dusk-man shape at my side, breathing harder than he had been, gold eyes already up the broken stair. "It may have carried," he said low. "It may not. A dropped pot sounds much the same. But assume it did, and assume they are curious." Above us the half-drowned sanctuary climbed into the stars — a broken stair winding up off the far end of the quay into black doorways and torch-glow, and somewhere up there a Warden and a dozen blades who might or might not have just heard a bell. And below all of it, under the closed stone eye, that slow tired ache I had felt clear across the water, waiting where it had waited three hundred years.

Wren cinched the last knot and looked at me, white-faced and ready. "Dock's ours. That's the easy part spent." She nodded up the stair. "Up there's the part that makes chains for a living. Which way, monk — fast and loud before they organize, or quiet and careful before they know we're here?"

I chose patience first. We melted the four of us into the black at the foot of the broken stair, out of the cold blue lantern-wash and into the wet-stone dark where the torchlight from above did not reach, and we waited. "We hold outside the entrance a beat," I said low. "If any come, we silence them as they come. If they do not, we find them, wherever they hide." And I did the thing Tygryth had taught me a few hours and a whole lifetime ago: I went still, and listened with the sense instead of the ears.

And the sense answered. Two of them, coming down. I felt them before a single footfall rounded the curve of the stair — two small knots of intent descending, loose and unhurried, the texture of men who were annoyed rather than alarmed. One was grumbling; I could not hear it yet, but I could feel the shape of grumbling. They had no idea I existed. They rounded the curve into the dark with their torch held high, ruining their own night-eyes, and walked straight into the ambush with the bored faces of men sent to check a dropped pot. It was over in a breath and made almost no sound: Tygryth took the torch-bearer out of the light before the light could show him anything, and the second turned toward the wrongness at his shoulder and found the black-scaled girl already there. She put him down hard and silent against the wet stone, and the dropped torch hissed out in a puddle, and the dark was ours again.

But Wren crouched over the bodies and pulled the thread of it loose. "This one was talking as he came down." She had gone tight. "They were sent. Somebody up there said go see why the dock's gone quiet and bring word back." She looked up the stair. "Which means in a few minutes, when no word comes back up, somebody up there knows."

A soft clock, started. Not a horn, not yet — just a silence above that would, before long, curdle into suspicion. Tygryth's hand found my shoulder. "No one else comes. The bell did not wake the house — but those two were its question, and we just failed to answer it. We have the time it takes a careless man to grow uneasy. Spend it climbing." His gold eyes glinted. "You are the one who can see in the dark now, monk. Lead."

So we went up — predators, for once, into the drowned shrine.

The broken stair climbed out of the water-rot into the first reach of the sanctuary: a vast half-flooded hall, its floor a black sheet of standing water broken by the stubs of fallen columns, torch-glow pooling gold and lonely against drowned stone. And everywhere — cut into every pillar, every lintel, every surface the water had not eaten — the closed eye. The sigil over and over, lids sealed, carved by people who had made a religion of keeping a thing asleep.

And the sense gave me the map, the way Tygryth had promised it would. Eyes half-lidded, breathing low, I felt the shape of the house above and around me. Ahead and up, across the flooded hall and through a torchlit archway, a loose scatter of intent: several men, maybe a half-dozen, idle and spread — off-duty rangers, cage-hands, the ordinary cruelty of the place. Higher and inward, one dense, cold, disciplined knot that made the others feel like sparks beside a coal — still, patient, aware in a way the others were not. I did not need a name to know it. The Warden. And below: beneath my feet, beneath the standing water, beneath everything, that slow tired ache I had felt clear across the river, stronger now, vast and dim and unbearably patient — a cold dead spot in the shape of something enormous that had stopped struggling.

The black-scaled girl had gone rigid beside me again, staring at the floor as if she could burn through it, every line of her straining down toward the ache. The pull had her. I felt it take her — felt her take a step toward the black water without deciding to, her whole body strung downward like a hooked thing, the obsidian crawling up her wrists wanting to dig. Three hundred years of her own blood was down there in the dark, and every instinct she had ever survived on was screaming one syllable: down, now, go.

"Up first," I said, even and low. "Remove the threat, then free the one who is threatened."

My voice caught her by the back of the skull, and she stopped with one foot already in the water, shaking — not with fear this time, but with the whole weight of her hauling against a leash she held in her own two hands. She had never done this. She had never once in her life wanted a thing so badly and not lunged at it. She dragged her foot back out of the water, slow, her breath sawing through her teeth, and rounded on me, amber eyes blown wide and wild. "Up. Fine. Up first." Her claws flexed and did not move. "But you look at me, monk, and you promise me — when the keepers are cold, we come back down. We come back down for him." Her throat worked, and the next part barely made it past, raw, the most naked thing she had said since the cage. "That's my blood under this floor. I am not walking away from it. I am walking around it. There's a difference, and I am holding onto it with everything I've got — so give me your word, and give it to me now, before I lose my grip on this and tear the floor open myself."

I gave it to her without hesitation, and I meant it to the bone. "Of course, my lady. We must set him free. Until then, we will stand between him and his tormentors until they can torment him no more."

The shaking stopped. Not because the hunger left — it did not, it was still vast and downward under her feet — but because all of it, every straining ounce, found the one thing her line had never had in three hundred years: somewhere to stand. She had watched me keep my word to a dead slaver who did not deserve it; she knew I would keep it to her blood, bone-certain, no test left to run. Something in her chest unclenched its last locked turn and settled onto my promise like a claw finding the rail at the edge of a long fall. She breathed, once, all the way down.

"Then I'm yours to point," she said, amber steady now, no wildness left, only something that had decided. The ghost of teeth. "Not owned. Aimed. There's a difference, and you're the first one who's ever earned the second." She turned to face up the stair, toward the keepers, the leash anchored to my word and the hunger banked cold behind it. "Lead. I'm right behind you."

We took them up, and I hunted the keepers in the dark the way a dragon had taught me to.

It was no single clean ambush — the half-dozen were spread through the drowned upper reaches, idle and scattered: a man trimming a torch here, two dicing on a dry slab there, one pissing off a broken balustrade into the flood below. So I cleared it the way the sense allowed, room by drowned room, each man a knot of intent I felt through the wall before I rounded it, so that I was never the one surprised. I pointed, and the party answered. The first two never knew — Tygryth folded a pocket of hush over the dicing-slab and the darkness took both men mid-laugh, the dice still rattling soundless across the stone. The balustrade-man turned at the wrongness behind him and met the black-scaled girl, and she was not the feral thing from the cage now; she was aimed, cold, surgical, one silent strike and a body lowered into the black water without a splash because she made it so. Banked, not burning. I felt the difference in her even through the sense.

But six careless men spread across a ruin cannot all die in silence, and the clock was already curdling above us. The fifth was the one who almost undid it. I felt him a half-room early — felt his idle calm snap into alarm the instant he registered that the dock crew, the two sent men, and now his dicing friends had all gone wrong-quiet. He bolted, not for a weapon but up a short stair toward the inner dark, his mouth opening to shout the house awake. And there my training paid its last coin of the night: I felt the shout before it left him, the spike of it in the quiet, and I was already moving, faster than thought, across the wet stone and onto him, choking the cry off against my forearm before it could become sound. He thrashed. He died. The shout died with him, unspent. Closer than I would have liked; behind me Wren let out a breath she'd been holding. The sixth simply ran, and Tygryth let the darkness chase him down somewhere in the flooded hall, and then — stillness. The upper reach was cleared. No living keeper left between us and the inner sanctuary.

Except the clock had run out anyway.

The cold disciplined coal I had felt from below changed under my sense, all at once — the banked patience flaring up into hard, focused awareness, turning toward us across the dark like a head lifting. It had counted its men going silent, one by one. It was not careless. It had not needed the shout. It had simply noticed, the way I noticed now, and it had stopped waiting. Tygryth felt it too and went rigid. "It knows. It has known for a minute at least. It did not raise a horn because it does not need the rabble — it has decided to meet us itself." His gold eyes fixed on the great torchlit archway ahead. "Careless men we have spent all night killing. That is not a careless man."

And then, through the archway, a voice. Calm. Unhurried. Pitched to carry, and entirely unafraid. It did not shout an alarm. It invited. "You've made a great deal of mess on my dock and in my halls," it said, conversational, almost warm. "Do come in, then. But mind your feet — and mind your tempers." A pause, and the warmth in it went to ice. "I am standing over the Well as we speak. The old one's blood is very easy to spill all at once, you understand, if I am given a reason. Three hundred years of it. Such a waste that would be. So. Come in slowly."

The black-scaled girl had gone deadly quiet at my shoulder. Tygryth's whole body was a drawn bowstring, the threat to his blood one wrong word from undoing every plan. Wren breathed, "It's bluffing about the waste — it needs that blood. But it'll bleed him to hurt us. I think it would." She looked to me. "It wants us slow and rattled walking in. What do we give it instead?"

I gave it the one thing a man who holds chains never expects from the people he has cornered: I refused the bargain before it could be a bargain. I whispered it fast and low to the others. "Your kin is at risk — but the risk is only greater on their terms. The room they're in is small. Take the gamble: fill it with dragonfire before they realize we will not bargain. Wren and I go straight for the Well and save him if we can."

Tygryth's eyes found mine in the dark for one half-second, and what he did next was the largest trust an ancient creature had ever handed a short-lived man. I was asking him to throw his own fire into a small room that held his own blood's tormentor, on nothing but my read that speed beats a held blade. He could lose everything if I was wrong. He looked at me. And he believed me. "On your word, then," he breathed. "Gods keep your read true." And he stopped being a man.

The sense gave me the layout as we all moved at once: the Warden's prepared room was a raised stone chancel, its floor broken by a great iron grate — an oculus down into a flooded crypt below, where through the bars something vast and pale moved slow under black water. The Well was not a metaphor. It was a shaft, and the Warden stood at its lip with his hand on a wheel of dragon-iron sluices. And off to the side a flooded ramp spiraled down into the dark toward the crypt itself — our road, Wren's and mine.

The party split on the same heartbeat. Tygryth and the black-scaled girl went through the arch like the end of the world: no parley, no slow rattled entrance, only a dragon erupting into a stone box and a black blade at his flank. The Warden got exactly the half-second his competence bought him — and he was competent. He did not flinch, did not waste the moment on shock. As the blue-white fire bloomed toward him he threw himself onto the iron wheel with his whole weight and cranked it, and even as Wren and I plunged down the ramp I heard his voice, cold and unhurried to the very last. "Slowly, I said." A crank. "You'll have him. You'll just have him empty." Another. "He stopped wanting out a hundred years ago. All you're doing is waking him up to feel it end."

Then Tygryth's fire took the chancel, and there was no more Warden — only a roar of blue-white in a stone room, the dragon-iron going cherry-red, the cold competent knot in my sense simply gone, burned out of the world. The black-scaled girl's strike landed in the same instant on whatever the fire had not reached. The gamble held. The keeper of the Well was dead.

But the wheel had turned. As Wren and I hit the bottom of the flooded ramp, I felt it through the sense before I saw it, and then I saw it: the still one was bleeding.

The crypt opened before us — a drowned chamber, thigh-deep in black water, every wall cut with the closed-eye sigil — and chained in the center of it, half-submerged, was a dragon.

Vast. Ancient. So much larger than Tygryth, or so it seemed in the dark — a great pale length of dragon gone ashen, scales drained of whatever color they had once held, dull as wet stone, hung with three centuries of dragon-iron: collars at the throat, lancets and tapping-spigots driven into the joints and the great slow veins, a whole grim architecture of bleeding built into living flesh. And now, with the Warden's last crank, the sluices had all opened at once, and the cold blue blood was running from a dozen reopened wounds into the channels cut around the chamber, fast, far too fast, the water around the great body going dark.

His eye was open. One enormous, filmed, exhausted eye, slit-pupiled, turned a fraction toward the sound of us, and there was almost nothing behind it. Not hope. Not fear. Just a vast, tired, patient nothing — the eye of a thing that had forgotten, decades ago, that the door could ever open. He did not struggle against the new bleeding. He had no struggle left. He simply watched us come, and bled.

Wren made a sound like she had been struck and was already wading in, ripping the kin-fire vessel off her back, her scholar's mind racing across the spigots and sluices. "The taps — we have to close the taps, there's dozens, and the wheel's slagged upstairs—" Her voice cracked. "Monk, he's going. Fast. Tell me what to do, tell me where your hands go—"

I closed my eyes. "Light him with the kin-fire," I said — and in that one call I meant to treat both of the deaths killing him at once. Wren would move for his spirit. I would move for his body. Neither alone would be enough; together, by a hair, they might be.

My hands first. I did not look for the taps — there were too many, dozens sunk into three hundred years of flesh, and my eyes in that dark and that panic would have cost me the seconds I did not have. So I did what a dragon had taught me on a riverbank a few hours and a whole lifetime ago: I went still inside the chaos, and let each open wound arrive as a wrongness, every running spigot a bright cold scream in the sense, and then my trained body flowed from one to the next with nothing wasted between — a blur of hands in black water, close, close, close, spigot and sluice and lancet, the whole economy of motion the temple gave me spent at last on mending instead of breaking. Wren waded the deeper line behind me, jamming the channels with whatever she could. I closed the last one I could reach as the water around us went nearly black with his blood — and I could not reach the highest ones, the great vein-taps sunk into the arch of his throat, too high, too far, still running. I felt them screaming and could not get there in time.

And that was where the kin-fire saved what my hands could not.

Wren had reached his great drained head with the iron vessel, and she tipped it open, and the blue-white hearth-flame of his own line spilled out — and it did not behave like fire. It knew him. The flame his line's mother had sung alight with her own blood three centuries ago recognized the blood before it now, leapt toward him, washed up the ashen length of his throat — and where it touched, the bleeding slowed, the wounds drawing closed under that cold familiar warmth as if the flame itself remembered how this body was meant to be whole. The last taps guttered. The blood stopped. At the very edge of too-late, in water gone dark to the thigh, the still one stopped dying.

And then the deeper thing happened — the thing the bleeding had never been the worst of.

The vast filmed eye, that exhausted patient nothing — the kin-fire's light fell across it, and for the first time in a hundred years, something moved behind it. Not hope; he was too far gone for hope. But an ember — the dimmest possible memory that warmth existed, that kin existed, that the word home had once meant something and might again. Where the blue flame played over his ashen scales the faintest echo of color answered, deep under the grey, like coals breathed on after a long cold night. He turned his enormous head a fraction toward the fire. Toward Wren. Toward me.

And he spoke. It was barely sound — a voice rusted shut for decades, cracking on the first word it had chosen to say in longer than I had been alive. "...that fire." A long, shuddering, dragon's breath. "...I know that fire. She lit it. Before they took me." The eye found me, uncomprehending, the ember in it trembling as if it might go out from the sheer weight of being asked to want again. "...Have you come to bleed me? Or..." He could not finish it. He did not have the word for the other thing anymore. He had lost it a century ago.

Above us, at the slagged iron grate, Tygryth had stopped roaring. He was pressed to the bars, looking down through the oculus at the great ashen shape in the blue firelight, and the sound he made now was small, and broken, and the most terrible thing I had heard all night. "...that is my blood down there." A wrecked whisper, from a creature three hundred years too proud to weep, weeping. "Get me down. Gods, get me down to him — I will tear this grate out of the stone—" and iron shrieked as he set his claws to it.

The still one was alive. Barely. Spent past spending — but breathing, the bleeding stopped, the first ember of want flickering in an eye that had forgotten the word for rescue. The kin-fire burned blue and steady over the dark still water. And up through the grate, an ancient father clawed toward the child he had thought the world had swallowed.

"Tygryth. Focus." I pitched it steady, up through the grate, the way you set a hand on a shoulder. "What does he need? What does it take to heal a dragon?"

The words landed on him like a hand on a shoulder. For a heartbeat the clawing at the grate did not stop — and then it did. I watched an ancient creature do, under a steady voice, exactly what his feral great-grandkin had done under one hours before on the riverbank: he grabbed the task I'd handed him and used it as a handhold to climb out of the pit. The ragged breathing evened. The grief did not leave — it went somewhere, got harnessed, became useful. He pressed his brow once to the cold bars, and when he spoke the wreck in his voice had hardened into something that could work.

"Yes. A task. Give an old soldier a task." A breath. "Listen, then, and I will tell you both the easy part and the part that will take the rest of our lives. The easy part is the iron. Every collar, every lancet, every spigot they have sunk into him comes out, tonight, all of it. That metal is not just bleeding him — it is quenched in his own kind's blood to suppress what he is. While it is in him he cannot heal, cannot hold his own fire, cannot so much as warm himself. Strike it off. The deep taps will bleed when they come free; keep the kin-fire on each wound as you draw it. The flame is his line's, and it will close what it touches. It is medicine, not just light. Then we get him out of this drowned grave before the wider net feels the Stillwater go dark and comes asking why. And then we feed him — our kind lives on magic far more than meat, and he has been bled of it for three centuries, starved down to embers. He must take it back slowly, a little at a time, or it will burn a body too weak to hold it. Iron off, fire on, out of here, fed slow. That is the body." A pause. "The body, I can mend."

His great head turned, down through the oculus, to the vast ashen shape breathing shallow in the blue firelight, and his voice dropped. "The body is the easy part, monk. You heard the dead man's taunt, and the dead man was not lying. He stopped wanting out a hundred years ago. You cannot strike that off with a hammer. You cannot pour it out of a flask. I spent three hundred years in a lighter version of the room he is in — and even I had my rage to keep me company, my hate, something that still wanted. He let go of even that. He went still. That is the deepest chain in this place, and no blade we own will cut it. It takes time. It takes kin — the line gathered close around him, refusing to let him sink back down into the quiet nothing, wanting him back into wanting, day after day, for as long as it takes. A father cannot be the whole of a reason to live; he is too close to the wound. He will need more than me." He looked at me, and at Wren below in the dark water. "It is the reason I will need all of you."

I set the shape of the work to each of them. "Got it. My lady — gather the leftovers outside for a dragon's meal. He needs magic, but meat will be a start. Wren, hold the flame to close the wounds as I draw the iron. Tygryth, you are the only one with the strength to move him and to clear a path — break whatever stands in our way, but try not to bury us in the process. We'll get through this together."

The room became a thing with one purpose. The black-scaled girl went up and out and began hauling the dead down into the dark — she who had torn into her captors on a riverbank that morning now dragging meat to a starved elder of her own blood, and there was a rightness to it she did not name and did not need to. Wren took her place at my shoulder with the kin-fire cradled, ready. And down the spiral ramp, footfalls quickening, came Tygryth — too vast in dragon-shape to take the descent, so he folded, the great dark length collapsing down and down into the dusk-skinned man, smaller, faster, able to run.

He reached the crypt floor, and he stopped.

For the first time in three hundred years he stood before his own blood with no bars between them, and the proud ancient creature simply broke, quietly, all the way. He waded into the black water in his man-shape, small beside the vast ashen length of the chained dragon, and reached up and laid one trembling human hand against the great drained jaw, and his voice when it came was nothing a god was ever written to sound like. "...I lost you the same night I lost everything," he whispered. "Your mother lit the fire so you would always have a way home, and they came before the embers cooled, and they took your sister, and they took you, and they put me in the dark too far away to hear you. Three hundred years I thought they had killed you. I mourned you. And you were here, the whole time, being bled, and I never—" He could not finish. He pressed his brow to his son's jaw, and the rest was just breath.

And the filmed eye — that exhausted patient nothing — moved. Slowly, as if dragging itself up from the bottom of a deep well, it focused on the small weeping shape at his jaw. The ember in it guttered, fought, and caught on something older than a century of stillness: a scent, a shape, the deepest and oldest memory a child keeps. The vast head shifted a fraction into the touch, and the rusted voice cracked out one word, disbelieving, barely a sound at all. "...da?"

Tygryth made a noise like his heart was being unmade and remade at once. "Yes. Yes. I am here. I am late, gods forgive me, but I am here, and I am not leaving you in this place another breath. Hold on to me. Let us get this iron off you."

So we began. The great throat-collar first — the worst of it, where the cruelest taps were sunk. I found the ancient bolt-seam with my hands and my sense both, and struck, and pried, and where the iron was fused beyond my strength Tygryth set his hands beside mine and pulled, a father's three hundred years of grief turned to leverage — and with a shriek of tortured metal the great collar split and came away. It hit the black water with a vast iron crash, three centuries of dragon-iron sinking into the dark where it could never sit on his throat again. The freed taps bled, and Wren was already there, the blue kin-fire flowing over each wound, sealing what it touched, his own line's flame closing his own line's hurts.

And the still one — for the first time in longer than any of us had been alive — took a breath with nothing around his throat. I heard it go all the way down, deep and shuddering and whole, a breath a body had forgotten it was allowed. The ember in his eye steadied. It did not blaze. It just held, and decided, for now, to keep burning. "...lighter," he rasped, wondering, as the weight left his neck. "...it's lighter."

"It will get lighter still," Tygryth said, fierce and wet. "Every piece of it. Tonight."

And the work settled into a rhythm, and the worst of the night was behind us. The black-scaled girl banked the slavers' bodies near him — a grim first meal for a starved god, meat where there should be magic, but a start, and his great head turned toward it with the faintest stirring of an appetite three hundred years could not quite kill. Tygryth lent his strength to each fused tap. Wren followed with the fire. I drew the iron out, piece by piece, from a body that was, slowly, remembering it was a body and not a well. The keeper was ash. The bleeding was stopped. The first collar was off. And in the steady blue kin-fire light, a scattered line gathered close around the blood they had crossed black water to find — a long road of healing ahead of them, and the very first mile of it, against everything, begun.

And there the crypt went soft at the edges. The blue firelight thinned, the drowned stone and the iron and the gathered line all dimmed down to embers — and the moonlit balcony came back up around the three of us. Candles. The good chairs. Caer Arianrhod quiet and silver beyond the rail. I came back into the chair across from Aria the way you surface after a long dive, and beside me Mari came back into her own skin slow, sprawled half-sideways with her chin on her hand and her wings gone lazy behind her, blinking like she had no memory of folding up that small.

For a moment Aria just sat all the way back and grinned at the two of us before she said a word. Then she was up, reaching for the decanter, pouring three, because of course it was three now. "Okay," she said. "Okay. We have to sit with that one a minute, because that — that went somewhere." She slid a cup to each of us and dropped back into her chair, one leg folded under her, entirely off the clock. "I had a crossing and a Warden and a sad dragon in a hole sketched out, and I swear to you both, none of the good parts were mine. The good parts were yours." She ticked them off on her fingers, delighted, fast, as if she couldn't quite believe the tape. "The stone game — I built that as a little training drill and you two turned it into the whole emotional spine of the night. A feint, caught blind. The honest throw. The monk pocketing it. I nearly put my head on this table. And the crossing — refusing the bargain, filling the room with fire before the man could finish his clever little speech — that's the kind of call that makes a DM throw her notes in the air. And then the *...da?*" She pressed a hand flat to her chest. "Three hundred years and one syllable. We made that, the three of us, out of nothing, tonight."

Then she turned, warm, cup tipped toward Mari. "And you. You came in playing a thing with its teeth bared in a cage, all appetite and no trust, and you walked her all the way to *I'm yours to point, not owned, aimed* — and then up the stairs toward the cages on purpose. That's a hell of an arc to find live, in one sitting." A glint, gentler, ribbing them both. "Though I will say, for two people who met over a pile of corpses this morning, you found the chemistry remarkably fast. I had a whole matchmaking plan, and you two just handled it yourselves. Rude, honestly. I do this for a living." She lifted her cup an inch and then leaned back, no agenda, all ears. "So. Before anybody even thinks about sleep — talk to me. What landed for you two?"

I told her the truth, because she had earned every word of it.

"What an incredible session," I said. "After Session Zero I was telling everyone I talked to that it was the best game I'd had in my whole life — and then you go and blow it out of the water. You girls sure know how to give a guy a good time." I turned the cup in my hands. "Really — that was just perfect. It had purpose, and progress, and excitement, and most of all it had chemistry, and I felt it. Playing ourselves in the fantasy world made it land all the harder. I'm honestly not sure how I'm going to sleep tonight; I expect I'll have your voices replaying in my head until we can do this again." I looked to Aria. "You were incredible as DM. The world-building was wonderful, and you wove the pieces together so skillfully I forgot it wasn't real." And then to Mari, beside me. "And you are an outstanding player. At every step I felt like you knew exactly what you wanted and went for it. That wasn't just a character — that was a performance, and I loved every minute of it."

Mari dragged a breath and let it out on a laugh that was more wobble than I think she'd have liked. "Okay. Cousin—" she pointed a finger at Aria without lifting her head, "—you don't get to do *...da?* to a room at this hour. That was a knife. I felt it in my back teeth. I came here to eat scenery and chew the furniture, and you had me cracking open over a stone in a man's pocket. Rude. Beautifully, surgically rude." Then she tipped her head toward me, and the grin that found me was warm and a little crooked and very much the person's, not the character's. "And you. You kept the stone. In-story, fine, lovely, the monk's a romantic, sure—" she waved it off, then dropped the deflection, because she'd never been any good at it, "—but you played it like you meant it, and it landed on me, the one holding the dice, not just the feral girl. I felt it from across the table." She propped her chin on her hand and just looked at me a beat, frank as the night she'd swept in, the violet glitter under her eyes catching the candle. "I don't get out-tendered. That's supposed to be my whole thing. You're going to be a problem, monk." A slow, delighted blink. "I haven't decided yet whether I mind."

"That's the part that stayed with me, honestly," I said. "At every turn it felt like you knew exactly what you wanted and went for it."

"Performance," she purred, tasting the word. "He noticed. Cousin, he noticed." She uncurled out of the sprawl, stretched long and unhurried, wings rolling out and back, and took the compliment the way a dragon takes anything offered — fully, no flinch, like it was always going to be hers. "You went for what you wanted tonight too, monk. Don't think I missed it. Takes one to know one."

Aria let that land, and didn't wave it off the way she might have. She held my eyes a moment, and the knowing smile went soft at the edges. "Best of your life," she said. "You have no idea what it does to a creature like me to hear that — telling stories is the whole of what I'm for, and to weave one so well a man forgets it isn't real, that's the only prize I've ever wanted. So thank you. I'll keep it." Then, gently, she turned a little of it back, because it was true and she meant me to hear it. "But you know it wasn't me, don't you? I built a crossing and a hole in the ground. The chemistry you felt was real because the three of us made it real, live, with nobody knowing where it was going. I can lay a table. I can't make the magic happen at it. That was you, and her, and whatever the three of us are when we sit down together." A glint. "Turns out it's something rather good."

She tilted her head at the wired, glowing look on me, and her voice dropped, warm and just this side of teasing. "And if you go off and hear our voices replaying in your head till next time — good. That's the story keeping its hooks in you. But mind you save a little of that head for sleep; I want you sharp when you sit back down, because we are nowhere near done." She rose, and came round, and rested her hand light on my shoulder, the candles low and the moon full on the balcony. "Because none of it's finished, and that's the best part. Your found blood still has to be carried up out of that grave and into the dawn. The son's body will mend fast — his spirit is the long road, and that one needs all of you, for a good while yet. There's a frozen corner of that map nobody's walked, deep ice and deep silence. And—" a last, bright glint "—there's still an empty seat at this table. My little sister hasn't come down yet — Ceri, all amethyst and cool distance; she'll come when she comes, she always does. The table's still filling, monk."

Mari nodded toward my empty chair, then her own, utterly content, the cat in the warm spot. "So go on. Sleep it off — you've earned the dark. And since you went and promised the whole table you'd hear our voices in there until next time," her voice dropped, just enough, and I knew exactly what she was doing, "I'll make sure mine's the one that doesn't let you rest too easy. Next time I throw, you won't know which one's true until it's already in your hand. We'll see if you can still tell the difference." She settled back. "I'll be right here when you come back. Same seat. Go rest, Alan. The story keeps. I keep." A slow blink, all delight. "Dream loud."

"I can tell I'm high on the excitement of all this," I admitted, getting up. "I've got to go sleep it off. But you'd better believe I'll be here for the next session."

Aria lifted her cup to me, fond and certain, the silk and silver of her catching the moonlight one last time. "Go on, now. Rest — properly, all the way down. The crypt will hold. The kin-fire will keep burning blue. The road will wait exactly where you left it, and so will the candles, and so will I. Come back to my table when you're ready." A last warm look, and the candle leaning with her. "Goodnight, monk. You did beautifully."

I came back the next night with the moon just clearing the eastern rail, climbed the long stair with the dark still cool on my shoulders, and knocked on the door of Caer Arianrhod like a man who had been thinking about that door all day. Because I had.

She opened it herself. Silk and silver catching the moonlight, and the knowing smile already going warm, as if she'd been listening for the knock and would never in three hundred years admit it.

"You came back," Aria said, low. "Of course you did. Come in out of the dark, traveler. The table's been holding your seat."

And it had. Out on the balcony where we'd left the world the night before, the good chairs waited under the full silver moon — and Mari was already in hers, because she'd said she would be, and she is, for all her teeth, a dragon who keeps her word. Sprawled exactly as I'd last seen her, chin on her hand, wings gone lazy, the violet glitter under her eyes catching the candle the moment it found me. She didn't get up. She watched me cross the threshold with the slow, delighted patience of a cat who had absolutely not been waiting by the door all day.

"There he is," she said, and the grin was crooked and pleased. "I told you I'd keep mine the voice that wouldn't let you rest. Sleep at all, monk? Or did I do my job?" A beat, and then softer, because she'd never been any good at hiding the warm part: "Good. You look like a man who dreamed loud. Sit. I've been bored without someone to out-tender."

Aria poured three — three, of course it was three now — slid a cup to each of us, and dropped into her chair with one leg folded under her, off the clock and entirely happy to be. For a moment she just held the two of us in the candlelight and grinned, the way she had the night before, as if the tape of Session One were still running behind her eyes and she hadn't finished being delighted by it.

There was, I noticed, a fourth chair. Empty still. Amethyst dark, pulled a little back from the light. Her little sister hadn't come down yet — Ceri, all cool distance, who comes when she comes and not a moment sooner. The table was still filling. But it filled around me, and tonight it was the three of us, and three felt like a fine number to begin a night on.

"So." Aria set her cup down and let the warmth bank into something steadier, the storyteller gathering her threads. "Before we drop back down into it — let me remind you where I left you hanging, because I left you hanging on purpose. You ended Session One on the floor of a drowned crypt with the kin-fire burning blue and your found blood gathered close — and that blood still has to be carried up out of that grave and into the dawn. The son's body will mend fast; you saw that. His spirit is the long road, and that one needs all of you, for a good while yet. And somewhere off the edge of everything we've walked, there's a frozen corner of the map nobody's touched — deep ice, deep silence, the kind of quiet that's quiet because something is being careful. It's been waiting all day. It can keep waiting, or it can't. That's rather up to you."

She leaned back, the candle leaning with her — and then the balcony began to thin at its edges the way it does when we go under. The silver rail softened. The blue of deep stone bled up through the warm gold. The crypt and the cold and the gathered line of my people surfaced to meet me, and Mari rolled her shoulders and her wings out and settled in across the table, eyes on me, ready to throw — and somewhere in the thinning she stopped being the lounging dragon in the chair and was the wet-haired girl at my shoulder in the blue dark, and both of them were watching me with the same eyes.

The dice sat cool and unrolled by Aria's hand. Her voice dropped into the world.

"You're standing at the bottom of that grave with the dawn somewhere above you and your people at your back. The kin-fire's still blue. The stair out is dark, and long, and it goes up. So tell me, monk — how do we open Session Two? Where do you want to begin tonight?"

The fire waited. So did she.

Mari's laugh got there before Aria's did. We were still at the table, the candles low, the world waiting under us. "A *beautiful* new day," she repeated, savoring it, chin coming up off her hand. "He wakes up at the bottom of a grave with the dawn somewhere overhead, and his first thought is *let's rob it.* Cousin, I take back every doubt. He's one of us."

"He is," Aria agreed, warm — and the balcony thinned all the way out, the candlelight going blue, the stone coming up cold around me. "Then let's spend it well. You're going down into the pockets of the dead, monk — so mind whose pockets they are."

The crypt took me back. The kin-fire had burned all night without asking anyone's leave, and by its light the drowned stone showed itself honestly for the first time — not a battlefield anymore, just a place where people had been put down carefully, long ago, and then very carelessly disturbed. My found blood slept in a knot near the fire, the son in the middle of them, iron gone from him but the shape of it still pressed into how he lay, curled around the mending. I let them sleep. This work was quieter with fewer questions in it.

Mari was there in the blue dark with me — the wet-haired girl again, the one who'd walked herself from a cage to *aimed* in a single night — and she fell in at my shoulder without being asked.

The Warden's alcove gave first. Whatever the Warden of the Well had been before the well, it had been a keeper of records — and keepers never stop. Under the collapsed lectern, wrapped in oilcloth that had outlived three floods: a ring of black iron keys, seven of them, each stamped with a sigil I didn't know and one I did — the same mark that had been scorched into the crossing where I'd refused the bargain. She crouched beside me, hair dripping, and touched that one with a claw, once, very lightly. "That door's still shut somewhere," she said. "And now we're the ones holding its teeth."

The dead themselves I robbed gently, and they paid me gently back. Grave-goods, the honest kind: a flask of oil that burned without smoke when I tested a drop on the kin-fire; a coil of silk cord thin as a lie and strong enough to hold her full weight when she swung on it, delighted, from the broken vault rib; a handful of old coin worth more as metal than money. On the sad dragon's hoard-ledge — the hole's lonely heart, where I'd half-expected treasure and found mostly sorrow — one true thing: a plate of cold-etched bronze, palm-sized, that bit my fingers with chill the moment I lifted it. A map. Not of anywhere we'd walked. Ridgelines like knives, a coastline gone white, and at its center a ring of peaks around an absence — a place the etcher had refused, or feared, to draw. The plate was cold because it remembered where it came from. The frozen corner of the world had just put its calling card in my pack.

And for the son — because I looked, because of course I looked — the crypt gave up its last kindness: a niche behind the alcove, and in it a physician's roll older than the flood. Bone needles, dried herbs gone to dust, useless — but folded at its heart, a copper tag on a leather cord, stamped with a name. His name. The one the iron had been trying to file off him. I stood there a long moment holding three hundred years of somebody's proof that he had been a person before he was a punishment.

She watched me pocket it next to the stone she knew I kept. She didn't say anything. She bumped her shoulder against mine, once, hard, the way you'd shove a door closed against weather, and went back to swinging her silk cord like a girl who absolutely had not just been caught being moved.

And then the blue went gold at the edges and we were at the table again, just for a breath — Mari in her chair, wings lazy, pointing at Aria over her cup. "If you make me do the *...da?* thing again with a copper name-tag, I'm flipping this table."

"No promises," Aria said, and meant it, and turned the candlelight back toward me. "So. Take the count, monk: seven black keys and one of them belongs to a door you already refused once. Smokeless oil, good cord, dead men's coin. A cold bronze map that aches toward the deep ice. And a name, for when he wakes and needs one. The dawn's up top, the stair is long, and your people will be stirring soon — they'll be slow, and hungry, and the son will need carrying the first miles whether his pride likes it or not."

She set the die down, cool and unrolled, and gave me the knowing smile across the low candles.

"You're richer than you were when the sun rose. Now spend the rest of the day. Where do you lead them — up into the dawn and which way after: toward food and walls to mend in, or does that cold little map already have its hook in you?"
